lessons.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
lessons.blurb_en: The Moon is always half lit. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see — explore it in 3D.
lessons.blurb_zh: 月亮永遠是一半亮的，改變的只是我們看得到多少亮面。用 3D 模型親手轉轉看。
lessons.big_idea_en: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon circles Earth, we see more or less of that lit half. That is all a phase is.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 太陽永遠照亮月亮的一半。月亮繞著地球轉，我們看到的亮面就時多時少——月相就只是這樣而已。

lab.how_en: Drag the space view to turn it, and scroll or pinch to zoom. Press Play, drag the slider, or tap a phase. The panel beside it shows what the Moon looks like from Earth at that moment.
lab.how_zh: 拖曳太空畫面可以旋轉視角，滾輪或雙指可以縮放。按「播放」、拖動滑桿或點選月相，旁邊的畫面就會顯示那一刻從地球看到的月亮。

legend.en: Teal ring: the half facing Earth
legend.zh: 青色環：朝向地球的半面

legend.en: The shape we see is where the two halves overlap.
legend.zh: 我們看到的月相，就是這兩個半面重疊的部分。

paras: Nearly a thousand years ago, the Song dynasty poet Su Shi wrote that people have their sorrows and joys, their partings and reunions, just as the Moon is sometimes hidden and sometimes bright, sometimes full and sometimes not. On Mid-Autumn night, families across Taiwan look up at a round, bright Moon. A week later, the same Moon looks like half a coin, and a week after that it seems to vanish from the sky. People have watched this cycle for as long as there have been people. The explanation is surprisingly simple, and it has nothing to do with the Moon itself changing shape.

The Moon makes no light of its own. Moonlight is really sunlight reflected off the Moon's gray, rocky surface. At every moment, the Sun lights up exactly one half of the Moon — the half that faces the Sun — while the other half stays dark. This is true on the night of a full moon, and it is just as true on a night when we cannot see the Moon at all. The Moon is always half lit. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth.

The Moon travels around Earth in an orbit, and as it moves, our view of its sunlit half keeps changing. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see almost nothing. This is the new moon. A few days later, a thin sliver of the lit half comes into view: a crescent. About a week after the new moon, we see exactly half of the disk lit. This phase is called the first quarter, because the Moon is a quarter of the way through its cycle. When Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, the whole lit half faces us, and we see a full moon. While the bright part is growing, we say the Moon is waxing; after the full moon it shrinks night by night, and we say it is waning. From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.

Many people, including many adults, believe the phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. It is an easy mistake to make, but it cannot be right. Earth's shadow always points directly away from the Sun, so the only time it can reach the Moon is at full moon, when the Moon is on the far side of Earth. When that happens, we see a lunar eclipse, which comes only a few times a year at most and is over within hours. Most months, the Moon slips just above or below the shadow, because its orbit is tilted by about five degrees. And a crescent moon hangs near the Sun in the sky, nowhere near Earth's shadow.

Because the cycle is so regular, people have used the Moon as a calendar for thousands of years. The traditional Chinese calendar begins each month on the day of the new moon, which is why the Mid-Autumn Festival, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, always comes near a full moon. The phases also tell you when to look up. A full moon rises around sunset and stays up all night. A first-quarter moon is already up in the afternoon, and a last-quarter moon rises around midnight and is still in the sky the next morning. So the Moon is not only a nighttime object. This week, try looking for it in daylight.
paras_zh: 將近一千年前，宋代詩人蘇軾寫下「人有悲歡離合，月有陰晴圓缺」。中秋夜，全台灣的家庭抬頭望著又圓又亮的月亮；一個星期後，同一個月亮看起來像半枚硬幣；再過一個星期，它好像從天空消失了。自有人類以來，人們就一直看著這個循環。它的道理其實出乎意料地簡單，而且跟月亮本身改變形狀一點關係也沒有。
月亮自己不會發光。所謂月光，其實是太陽光照在月球灰色岩石表面後反射出來的光。任何時刻，太陽都剛好照亮月球的一半——朝向太陽的那一半——另一半則是暗的。滿月那晚是這樣，完全看不到月亮的那晚也一樣。月亮永遠是一半亮、一半暗；會改變的，是我們從地球上能看到那亮的一半有多少。

月亮沿著軌道繞地球運行，它一移動，我們看到它亮面的角度就跟著改變。當月亮走到地球和太陽之間，亮的那一半背對著我們，我們幾乎什麼都看不到，這就是新月（朔）。幾天後，亮面的一小條細邊轉進視野，這就是眉月。新月後大約一週，我們看到月面剛好亮了一半，稱為上弦月——英文叫 first quarter，因為月亮這時走完了一個循環的四分之一。當地球位在太陽和月亮之間，整個亮面都朝向我們，就是滿月（望）。亮的部分一天天變大時，我們說月亮在「盈」（waxing）；滿月之後一夜一夜變小，就是「虧」（waning）。從一次新月到下一次新月，大約是 29.5 天。

很多人——包括很多大人——以為月相是地球的影子落在月亮上造成的。這個誤會很容易發生，但它不可能是對的。地球的影子永遠指向背對太陽的方向，所以它唯一能碰到月亮的時候，是月亮走到地球另一側的滿月時。真的碰到了，我們看到的是月食——一年最多只有幾次，而且幾個小時內就結束。大多數月份，月亮會從影子的上方或下方擦身而過，因為它的軌道傾斜了大約五度。何況眉月掛在天空中離太陽不遠的地方，跟地球的影子根本八竿子打不著。
因為這個循環非常規律，幾千年來人們一直把月亮當成日曆。傳統農曆把每個月的第一天訂在新月（朔）那天，所以農曆八月十五的中秋節，永遠落在滿月前後。月相也告訴你什麼時候該抬頭看。滿月大約在日落時升起，整夜都在天上；上弦月下午就已經升上天空；下弦月大約半夜才升起，到隔天早上都還看得到。所以月亮不只是晚上的東西——這個星期，試著在白天找找看它吧。
questions: Why is the Moon always "half lit," even on a night when we cannot see it?
Where is the Moon at new moon, and why can't we see it then?
Give two reasons why Earth's shadow cannot be what causes the Moon's phases.
answers: Because the Sun always shines on the half of the Moon that faces it. The Moon's position only changes how much of that lit half is turned toward Earth.
It is between Earth and the Sun, so its lit half faces away from us and the side facing Earth is dark. It is also in the sky with the Sun, lost in its glare.

Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, so it can only reach the Moon at full moon, and when it does we see a lunar eclipse, not a phase. Also, a crescent moon appears close to the Sun in the sky, far from Earth's shadow.

phases.when_zh: 看不到：它和太陽一起走過天空，被陽光淹沒。

phases.when_zh: 日落後不久，低掛在西方天空。

phases.when_zh: 下午到上半夜，約午夜落下。右半邊亮。

phases.when_zh: 傍晚前升起，一直到過了午夜。

phases.when_zh: 整夜可見：日落時升起，日出時落下。

phases.when_zh: 黎明前，低掛在東方天空。

lessons.phases_note_en: Directions and "right/left" are for the Northern Hemisphere, where Taiwan is. Times are rough: the real times shift by an hour or more with the seasons.
lessons.phases_note_zh: 方向與左右以北半球（台灣所在）為準。時間只是大概，實際會隨季節前後差一個小時以上。

myths.myth_en: The phases are caused by Earth's shadow.
myths.myth_zh: 月相是地球的影子造成的。
myths.fact_en: Earth's shadow can only reach the Moon at full moon, and then it makes a lunar eclipse, not a phase. Turn on "Earth's shadow" in the model and watch where it points.
myths.fact_zh: 地球的影子只有在滿月時才可能落到月亮上，那時造成的是月食，不是月相。在模型裡打開「地球的影子」，看看它指向哪裡。

myths.myth_en: The Moon only comes out at night.
myths.myth_zh: 月亮只有晚上才出來。
myths.fact_en: For about half of every month, the Moon is up in daylight too. A first-quarter moon is easy to spot in the afternoon.
myths.fact_zh: 每個月大約有一半的日子，白天也看得到月亮；上弦月在下午就很容易找到。

myths.myth_en: The far side of the Moon is always dark.
myths.myth_zh: 月球背面永遠是黑的。
myths.fact_en: The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side; at new moon it is fully lit. We never see it only because the Moon turns exactly once for every trip around Earth, so the same face always points at us.
myths.fact_zh: 月球背面照到的陽光跟正面一樣多，新月時背面甚至是全亮的。我們看不到它，只是因為月亮每繞地球一圈剛好自轉一圈，永遠同一面朝向我們。

myths.myth_en: People in other countries see a different phase tonight.
myths.myth_zh: 別的國家今晚看到的是不同的月相。
myths.fact_en: Everyone on Earth sees the same phase at the same time. In the Southern Hemisphere, though, the Moon looks upside down, so a waxing moon is lit on the left. Try the "Southern Hemisphere" switch.
myths.fact_zh: 同一時間，全世界看到的月相都一樣。不過在南半球，月亮看起來是上下顛倒的，所以漸盈的月亮是左邊亮。試試模型裡的「南半球」開關。

tricks.body_en: The lit side of the Moon always points toward the Sun. It works in any country, at any hour, in either hemisphere.
tricks.body_zh: 月亮的亮面永遠朝向太陽。不管在哪個國家、幾點鐘、南半球還是北半球，都成立。

tricks.title_zh: 中文口訣：上上上西西，下下下東東
tricks.body_en: First quarter (上弦): first half of the lunar month, first half of the night, western sky, western half lit. Last quarter (下弦): the second half of each, and east instead of west.
tricks.body_zh: 上弦月：農曆上半月、上半夜看得到、在西邊天空、西半邊亮。下弦月：農曆下半月、下半夜看得到、在東邊天空、東半邊亮。

tricks.body_en: In the Northern Hemisphere the Moon grows like a D, is full like an O, and shrinks like a C. Flip it in the Southern Hemisphere.
tricks.body_zh: 在北半球，月亮變大時像 D、滿月像 O、變小時像 C；到了南半球要反過來。

tricks.title_zh: 為什麼台灣的眉月像在微笑
tricks.body_en: Near the tropics, and Taiwan sits right on the Tropic of Cancer, a crescent low in the sky often lies on its back like a smile or a little boat. Farther north, it stands up more like a D or a C.
tricks.body_zh: 在熱帶附近（台灣就在北回歸線上），貼近地平線的眉月常常像躺著的微笑或小船；越往北走，它就越像立起來的 D 或 C。

activity.title_en: Be the Earth: A Lamp-and-Ball Moon
activity.title_zh: 你就是地球：燈泡與小球的月相實驗

materials.en: A lamp with the shade removed (the Sun)
materials.zh: 一盞拿掉燈罩的檯燈（太陽）

materials.en: A white foam ball stuck on a pencil (the Moon)
materials.zh: 插在鉛筆上的白色保麗龍球（月亮）

materials.en: Your own head (Earth)
materials.zh: 你自己的頭（地球）

materials.en: A room you can make dark
materials.zh: 一間可以關燈的教室

steps.en: Turn off the room lights and stand a few steps from the lamp. Hold the ball at arm's length, a little higher than your head.
steps.zh: 關掉教室的燈，站在離檯燈幾步遠的地方。手臂伸直拿著小球，比頭稍微高一點。

steps.en: Face the lamp with the ball in front of it. You see only the dark side: a new moon.
steps.zh: 面向檯燈，讓小球擋在燈前面：你只看到暗的一面——這是新月。

steps.en: Keep your eyes on the ball and turn slowly to your left. A crescent appears on its right edge, then a half, then more.
steps.zh: 眼睛盯著小球，慢慢向左轉。右邊先出現一道細細的眉月，接著是半個，然後越來越多。

steps.en: With your back to the lamp (hold the ball above your head's shadow), you see a full moon. Keep turning and watch it wane.
steps.zh: 背對檯燈時（讓小球高過頭的影子），你看到的是滿月。繼續轉，看它一點一點虧下去。

steps.en: Ask yourself: was the ball ever not half lit? What really changed?
steps.zh: 問問自己：小球有哪一刻不是一半亮的嗎？真正改變的是什麼？

activity.tip_en: Teaching tip: before each quarter turn, have students predict what they will see. If a head shadow falls on someone's ball, stop and point it out: that is a lunar eclipse.
activity.tip_zh: 教學提示：每轉四分之一圈前，先讓學生預測會看到什麼。如果有人的頭影剛好遮到小球，停下來告訴大家：這就是月食。

lessons.title: Why Isn't There an Eclipse Every Month?
lessons.title_zh: 為什麼不是每個月都有日食月食？
lessons.blurb_en: Solar and lunar eclipses, the Moon's tilted orbit, and eclipse seasons, with a 3D model that runs on real dates.
lessons.blurb_zh: 日食、月食、傾斜的月球軌道與「食季」；3D 模型照真實日期運轉，算得出下一次日月食。
lessons.big_idea_en: An eclipse needs the Sun, Earth, and the Moon in a nearly perfect line. The Moon's orbit is tilted, so that happens only twice a year, during eclipse seasons.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 日月食需要太陽、地球、月亮幾乎排成一直線。月球軌道是傾斜的，所以這種機會一年只有兩次，叫做「食季」。

lab.title_zh: 真實日期，真實的日月食

legend.zh: 青色圈：月球軌道（實線在黃道面上方，虛線在下方）

legend.zh: 金色菱形：交點，月球軌道穿過黃道面的兩個點

legend.zh: 深色錐：地球與月亮的影子，永遠指向背對太陽的方向

legend.zh: 時間軸上的金色帶：食季

lab.scale_en: In the 3D view, the tilt of the Moon's orbit (really 5.1°) and the sizes of the Sun, Earth, and Moon as seen from each other are all drawn about five times larger, so the shadows look wider and linger about five times longer there. Whether an eclipse happens does not change. The two small views show the real Sun and Moon, and every dot on the timeline is a real eclipse.
lab.scale_zh: 3D 畫面裡，月球軌道的傾斜（實際 5.1°）以及日、地、月彼此看到的大小，全都放大了約五倍，所以影子看起來比較寬、停留時間也長了約五倍；但「會不會發生食」完全不受影響。右邊兩個小畫面是真實的太陽與月亮，時間軸上的每一個點都是真正的日月食。

paras: In ancient China, people said that a heavenly dog was eating the Sun. When daylight suddenly faded in the middle of the day, crowds beat drums and banged pots to scare the dog away, and it always seemed to work, because the Sun always came back. Chinese court astronomers took eclipses so seriously that they kept records of them for more than two thousand years. Today we know that no dog is involved. An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and the Moon line up almost perfectly, so that one of them moves into another's shadow.

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth and its shadow falls on Earth. This can only happen at new moon, when the Moon is on the Sun's side of Earth. By a lucky coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost exactly the same size in our sky. When the Moon covers the Sun completely, day turns to twilight for a few minutes, and the Sun's glowing outer atmosphere, the corona, appears around the black Moon. The darkest part of the Moon's shadow is never more than about 270 kilometers wide, though, so only people inside that narrow path see a total eclipse. People for thousands of kilometers around it see a partial eclipse, with a bite taken out of the Sun.

The Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle. If a solar eclipse happens while the Moon is farther from Earth than usual, the Moon looks slightly smaller than the Sun and cannot cover it completely, so a bright ring of sunlight is left around the dark Moon. This is an annular eclipse, from the Latin word for a ring. On June 21, 2020, the path of one crossed Taiwan, and people in Chiayi and Tainan saw a thin "ring of fire." Whatever kind of solar eclipse it is, never look straight at the Sun, not even when most of it is covered. Use certified eclipse glasses, or make a simple pinhole viewer and watch the Sun's image on a sheet of paper.

A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon and the Moon moves into Earth's shadow. This can only happen at full moon. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is visible to everyone on the night side of Earth at the same time, and it is perfectly safe to watch with your bare eyes. During a total lunar eclipse the Moon does not disappear. It turns a dark copper red, because Earth's atmosphere bends a little sunlight into the shadow and filters out most of the blue light, just as it does at sunset. In a sense, the red Moon is lit by all of Earth's sunrises and sunsets at once.

If the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun every month, why isn't there a solar eclipse every month? The answer is that the Moon's orbit is tilted by about five degrees compared with Earth's path around the Sun. Most months, the new moon passes a little above or below the Sun, and its shadow misses Earth; two weeks later, the full moon passes above or below Earth's shadow. The two paths cross at only two points, called nodes, and an eclipse can happen only when a new or full moon falls close to one of them. That happens during a window of about five weeks, roughly every six months, called an eclipse season. The Sun's path across our sky is even named the ecliptic, because eclipses can happen only when the Moon is near it.

Every year has at least two solar eclipses somewhere on Earth, and lunar eclipses are about as common. Yet most people see many more lunar eclipses than solar ones. A lunar eclipse can be seen from half the planet, while a total solar eclipse touches only a thin strip, so any one place waits, on average, about 375 years between total solar eclipses. That is why people travel across the world to stand in the Moon's shadow, even for two or three minutes.
paras_zh: 古時候的中國人說，是天上的狗在吃太陽——「天狗食日」。大白天天色忽然暗下來時，人們擂鼓、敲鍋，要把天狗嚇跑；而且好像每次都有效，因為太陽總會回來。中國朝廷的天文官非常看重日食，兩千多年來持續把它們記錄下來。今天我們知道，這件事跟狗一點關係也沒有：當太陽、地球、月亮幾乎排成一直線，其中一個走進另一個的影子裡，就發生了「食」。

日食，是月亮剛好走到太陽和地球中間，把影子投在地球上。這只可能發生在新月（朔），也就是月亮位在地球朝向太陽那一側的時候。很巧的是，太陽的直徑大約是月亮的 400 倍，但距離也遠了大約 400 倍，所以兩者在天空中看起來幾乎一樣大。當月亮把太陽完全遮住，白天會暗成黃昏般好幾分鐘，太陽發光的外層大氣——日冕——會在黑色的月亮周圍現身。不過月影最黑的核心，寬度從來不超過約 270 公里，只有站在這條狹長路徑裡的人才看得到日全食；方圓幾千公里內的人只看到日偏食，太陽像被咬掉一口。

月球的軌道不是正圓。如果日食發生時月亮離地球比平常遠，它看起來就比太陽小一點，遮不滿，黑色月亮周圍會留下一圈明亮的陽光——這就是日環食，英文 annular 來自拉丁文的「環」。2020 年 6 月 21 日，就有一次日環食的路徑橫越台灣，嘉義、台南的民眾看到了細細的「火環」。不管是哪一種日食，都絕對不要直視太陽，就算大部分被遮住也一樣。請使用合格的日食觀測眼鏡，或是做一個簡單的針孔投影器，看投在紙上的太陽影像。
月食，是地球剛好走到太陽和月亮中間，月亮走進地球的影子裡。這只可能發生在滿月（望）。跟日食不同，月食發生時，地球上所有處在夜晚的人都能同時看到，而且用肉眼直接看完全安全。月全食時月亮並不會消失，而是變成暗暗的古銅紅色：因為地球的大氣把一點點陽光折進影子裡，又濾掉大部分的藍光——跟夕陽變紅是同一個道理。某種意義上，那顆紅月亮，是被地球上所有的日出和日落同時照亮的。

如果月亮每個月都會經過地球和太陽之間，為什麼不是每個月都有日食？答案是：月亮的軌道和地球繞太陽的軌道之間，傾斜了大約五度。大多數月份，新月從太陽的稍上方或稍下方經過，月影落不到地球；兩週後的滿月，也從地球影子的上方或下方通過。兩條軌道只在兩個點相交，稱為「交點」；只有新月或滿月剛好落在交點附近，才會發生日食或月食。這樣的時機大約每六個月出現一次，每次約五週，稱為「食季」。太陽在天空中走的路徑叫做 ecliptic（黃道），名字正是來自 eclipse：因為只有月亮走到這條線附近，才可能發生食。
地球上每年至少會發生兩次日食，月食也差不多一樣常見。但大多數人看過的月食，遠比日食多。月食時，半個地球都看得到；日全食卻只掃過一條細細的帶子，平均而言，地球上任何一個地點要等大約 375 年，才會再遇到一次日全食。這就是為什麼有人願意飛越大半個地球，只為了站進月亮的影子裡兩三分鐘。
questions: Why can a solar eclipse happen only at new moon, and a lunar eclipse only at full moon?
Why does the Moon turn red during a total lunar eclipse instead of disappearing?
Why isn't there an eclipse every month?
answers: A solar eclipse needs the Moon between the Sun and Earth, which is where the Moon is at new moon. A lunar eclipse needs Earth between the Sun and the Moon, which is where the Moon is at full moon.
Earth's atmosphere bends some sunlight into the shadow and filters out most of the blue light, so reddish light, like the light of sunrise and sunset, still reaches the Moon.

The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so most new and full moons pass above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow. An eclipse happens only when a new or full moon falls near a node, during an eclipse season about every six months.

myths.myth_en: There is an eclipse every month.
myths.myth_zh: 每個月都有日食、月食。
myths.fact_en: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so most new and full moons miss. Eclipses cluster in two eclipse seasons a year. Press Play in the model and watch the shadows pass above and below.
myths.fact_zh: 月球軌道是傾斜的，大多數新月和滿月都會錯過。日月食集中在一年兩次的食季。在模型裡按「播放」，看影子一次次從上方或下方擦過。

myths.myth_en: Everyone on the day side of Earth sees a solar eclipse.
myths.myth_zh: 只要是白天的地方，都看得到日食。
myths.fact_en: Only places inside the Moon's shadow see it. A thin path sees it total, a wide region around it sees it partial, and the rest of the day side sees nothing at all.
myths.fact_zh: 只有在月影範圍內才看得到：狹長的一條看到全食，周圍一大片看到偏食，其餘白天的地方什麼都看不到。

myths.myth_en: Food cooked during an eclipse is poisonous, and pregnant women should hide.
myths.myth_zh: 日食時煮的東西有毒，孕婦要躲起來。
myths.fact_en: Nothing about sunlight changes during an eclipse, and no special rays harm food or babies. The only real danger is looking straight at the Sun and hurting your eyes.
myths.fact_zh: 日食時陽光本身沒有任何改變，也沒有什麼特殊射線會傷害食物或胎兒。真正的危險只有一個：直視太陽會傷眼睛。

myths.myth_en: Very dark sunglasses are good enough for watching a solar eclipse.
myths.myth_zh: 戴很黑的太陽眼鏡就能看日食。
myths.fact_en: Even dark sunglasses let through thousands of times too much light. Use eclipse glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 standard, or a pinhole viewer.
myths.fact_zh: 再黑的太陽眼鏡，透進來的光仍然強了幾千倍。請用符合 ISO 12312-2 標準的日食眼鏡，或針孔投影器。

tricks.title_en: Solar at new, lunar at full
tricks.title_zh: 日食在初一，月食在十五
tricks.body_en: A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon, and a lunar eclipse only at full moon. The Chinese calendar starts every month at the new moon, so a solar eclipse falls on the first day of a lunar month (or the day next to it, if it happens right around midnight), and a lunar eclipse falls around the fifteenth.
tricks.body_zh: 日食一定發生在新月（朔），月食一定發生在滿月（望）。農曆每個月從朔開始，所以日食就在初一（剛好發生在午夜前後時，可能落在相鄰那一天），月食在十五前後。

tricks.title_en: Name the one in the middle
tricks.title_zh: 誰在中間，就是誰的影子
tricks.body_en: Moon in the middle: the Moon's shadow falls on Earth, and that is a solar eclipse. Earth in the middle: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, and that is a lunar eclipse.
tricks.body_zh: 月亮在中間，月影落在地球上，是日食；地球在中間，地影落在月亮上，是月食。

tricks.body_en: An eclipse season lasts about five weeks, so a solar eclipse is often followed or preceded by a lunar eclipse two weeks apart. Look for pairs of dots on the timeline.
tricks.body_zh: 一個食季大約五週，所以日食前後兩週常常跟著一次月食。在時間軸上找找看成對的圓點。

tricks.body_en: A lunar eclipse is always safe, and you need no equipment. Never look straight at a solar eclipse without certified eclipse glasses. Ordinary sunglasses, however dark, are not enough.
tricks.body_zh: 月食永遠安全，不需要任何裝備。日食沒有合格的日食眼鏡，就絕對不要直視；一般太陽眼鏡再黑都不夠。

activities.title_en: Eclipses with a Lamp and a Ball
activities.title_zh: 燈泡與小球做日食月食

materials.en: A lamp with the shade removed (the Sun)
materials.zh: 一盞拿掉燈罩的檯燈（太陽）

materials.en: A white foam ball stuck on a pencil (the Moon)
materials.zh: 插在鉛筆上的白色保麗龍球（月亮）

materials.en: Your own head (Earth)
materials.zh: 你自己的頭（地球）

materials.en: A room you can make dark
materials.zh: 一間可以關燈的教室

steps.en: Set up as in Lesson 1: the lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Moon, and your head is Earth.
steps.zh: 照第一課布置：檯燈是太陽，小球是月亮，你的頭是地球。

steps.en: Face the lamp and move the ball until it hides the bulb. Its shadow falls on your face: a solar eclipse. Close one eye; the eye in the darkest part of the shadow sees it total.
steps.zh: 面向檯燈，移動小球直到它擋住燈泡：球的影子落在你臉上——這是日食。閉上一隻眼，站在影子最黑處的那隻眼看到的就是全食。

steps.en: Turn around so the lamp is behind you, and move the ball into your head's shadow: a lunar eclipse.
steps.zh: 轉身背對檯燈，把小球移進你頭的影子裡——這是月食。

steps.en: Now raise your arm a little, as if the Moon's orbit were tilted, and go around again. The ball passes above the bulb and above your head's shadow: no eclipses this month.
steps.zh: 現在把手臂抬高一點，像是月球軌道傾斜了，再轉一圈：小球從燈泡上方、也從頭影上方經過——這個月沒有日月食。

steps.en: For older students: keep your arm tilted toward the same wall of the room and walk slowly in a circle around the lamp. At two places in your walk, the ball lines up with the lamp again: those are the two eclipse seasons.
steps.zh: 給大一點的學生：手臂一直斜向教室的同一面牆，繞著檯燈慢慢走一圈。走到兩個地方時，小球會再度跟燈泡對齊——那就是一年兩次的食季。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: step 5 is exactly what the Whole year view of the 3D model shows. Let students walk it first, then open the model.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：第 5 步就是 3D 模型「全年」視角畫的東西。先讓學生親身走一次，再打開模型。

materials.en: Two sheets of stiff white card
materials.zh: 兩張較硬的白色卡紙

materials.en: A piece of aluminum foil
materials.zh: 一小張鋁箔

materials.en: Tape and a pin
materials.zh: 膠帶和一根大頭針

steps.en: Cut a square hole about 3 centimeters wide in the middle of one card, and tape the foil over it.
steps.zh: 在一張卡紙中央剪一個約 3 公分的方洞，用膠帶把鋁箔貼在洞上。

steps.en: Poke one small, clean hole in the foil with the pin.
steps.zh: 用大頭針在鋁箔上戳一個乾淨的小洞。

steps.en: Stand with your back to the Sun. Hold up the foil card so that sunlight passes through the pinhole onto the second card.
steps.zh: 背對太陽站好，舉起貼鋁箔的那張卡，讓陽光穿過針孔落在另一張卡紙上。

steps.en: The small bright circle is an image of the Sun. Move the second card farther away to make it bigger. During a partial eclipse, you will see the bite.
steps.zh: 那個明亮的小圓就是太陽的影像；把第二張卡紙拿遠一點，影像會變大。日偏食時，你會看到它缺了一角。

activities.tip_en: Never look at the Sun through the pinhole. No card handy? During a partial eclipse, look at the ground under a leafy tree: the gaps between the leaves act as pinholes and paint hundreds of little crescent Suns.
activities.tip_zh: 絕對不要透過針孔看太陽。手邊沒有卡紙？日偏食時看看樹蔭底下：葉縫就是天然的針孔，地上會出現幾百個小小的月牙形太陽。

lessons.title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
lessons.blurb_en: It is the tilt, not the distance. Follow Earth around the Sun on real dates, and watch Taiwan's days grow long and short.
lessons.blurb_zh: 原因是傾斜，不是距離。跟著真實日期繞太陽一圈，看台灣的白天一天天變長、變短。
lessons.big_idea_en: Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not from its distance to the Sun. The tilt gives each hemisphere a higher Sun and longer days in turn.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 四季來自地軸的傾斜，不是地球離太陽的遠近。傾斜讓南北半球輪流得到更高的太陽和更長的白天。

lab.how_en: The model puts Earth where it really is on any date, with its axis tilted 23.4° and always pointing at the North Star. Press Play to run through the year, switch to Close-up to watch day and night move across Taiwan, or turn off the tilt to see what Earth would be like without seasons.

legend.zh: 金色虛線：南北回歸線；藍色虛線：南北極圈

legend.en: Glowing dot: where the noon Sun is straight overhead

legend.en: White line: Earth's axis, always pointing at the North Star
legend.zh: 白線：地軸，永遠指向北極星

lab.scale_en: Not to scale. Earth and the Sun are both drawn far too big for the size of the orbit, and the Sun, which is really 109 times wider than Earth, is drawn only about twice as wide. The dates, the tilt, and the shape of the orbit are real: the orbit really is this close to a circle.
lab.scale_zh: 大小未按比例：地球和太陽相對於軌道都畫得太大；太陽實際上比地球寬 109 倍，這裡只畫了約 2 倍。日期、傾角與軌道形狀都是真實的——地球的軌道真的就這麼接近正圓。

paras: Ask a room full of people why summer is hot, and many will say it is because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. It sounds reasonable, but it cannot be right. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of winter in Taiwan. And when it is summer in Taiwan, it is winter in Australia, even though both countries are the same distance from the Sun. The real reason for the seasons is not distance. It is a tilt.

Earth spins around an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, called its axis. The axis is not straight up and down compared with Earth's path around the Sun. It is tilted by about 23.5 degrees. Just as important, the axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year, toward the North Star, Polaris. So as Earth travels around the Sun, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun for half of the year and away from it for the other half.

Leaning toward the Sun does two things. First, the Sun climbs higher in the sky. When sunlight comes from high overhead, it strikes the ground straight on, and its energy is concentrated on a small area. When the Sun is low, the same sunlight is spread across a much larger area, like a flashlight beam shining on a table at a slant. Second, the days get longer. In Changhua, the Sun is up for more than 13 and a half hours in late June but only about 10 and a half hours in late December. More hours of stronger sunlight add up to summer.

Four dates mark the turning points. Around June 21, the summer solstice, the Northern Hemisphere leans most toward the Sun, and at noon the Sun stands straight overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5 degrees north of the equator. The Tropic of Cancer runs right through Taiwan, through Chiayi and Hualien, so on that day a pole standing there at noon casts almost no shadow. Around December 21, the winter solstice, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, far to the south. Halfway between, around March 20 and September 23, come the equinoxes, when day and night are almost equal everywhere on Earth.

Long before anyone knew why, Chinese farmers tracked the seasons with great care. The traditional calendar divides the Sun's yearly path into 24 solar terms, each about 15 days long, with names like Grain Rain, White Dew, and Frost's Descent. The solstices and equinoxes are four of them. Because the solar terms follow the Sun rather than the Moon, they fall on nearly the same dates every year, which made them a reliable guide for planting and harvest. In 2016, UNESCO added them to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

One last puzzle: if the Sun is highest in June, why are July and August the hottest months in Taiwan? Oceans and land take weeks to warm up, the way a pot of water takes a while to boil after you turn on the stove, so the warmest weather lags behind the strongest sunlight. The same delay makes January and February colder than December. And in the Southern Hemisphere, everything is reversed: in Australia, many families spend Christmas at the beach.
paras_zh: 問一屋子的人夏天為什麼熱，很多人會說：因為夏天地球離太陽比較近。聽起來很合理，但它不可能是對的。地球其實在 1 月初離太陽最近，那時台灣正是冬天。而且台灣過夏天的時候，澳洲正在過冬天，兩個國家離太陽的距離明明一樣。四季真正的原因不是距離，而是一個傾斜。
地球繞著一條穿過南北極的假想線自轉，這條線叫做地軸。跟地球繞太陽的軌道相比，地軸不是直立的，而是傾斜了大約 23.5 度。同樣重要的是：地軸整年都指向太空中的同一個方向——北極星。所以地球繞太陽運行時，北半球有半年傾向太陽、另外半年背向太陽。
傾向太陽會帶來兩件事。第一，太陽在天空中爬得更高。陽光從高處照下來時，是正面打在地上，能量集中在一小塊面積上；太陽低的時候，同樣的陽光攤在大得多的面積上，就像手電筒斜斜照在桌上一樣。第二，白天變長了。在彰化，六月下旬太陽在天上超過 13 個半小時，十二月下旬卻只有大約 10 個半小時。更長的時間、更強的陽光，加起來就是夏天。
有四個日子是轉折點。6 月 21 日前後是夏至，北半球最傾向太陽，正午太陽直射北回歸線，也就是赤道以北約 23.5 度的地方。北回歸線正好穿過台灣的嘉義和花蓮，所以那天正午，豎在那裡的竿子幾乎沒有影子。12 月 21 日前後是冬至，太陽直射遙遠南方的南回歸線。兩者中間的 3 月 20 日和 9 月 23 日前後，是春分和秋分，那時全世界的晝夜幾乎一樣長。
早在有人知道原因之前，中國的農民就非常仔細地觀察季節。傳統曆法把太陽一年走過的路分成二十四個節氣，每個大約十五天，有穀雨、白露、霜降這樣的名字；夏至、冬至、春分、秋分就是其中四個。因為節氣跟著太陽走、不是跟著月亮走，每年幾乎落在同樣的日期，所以成了播種與收成可靠的指南。2016 年，聯合國教科文組織把二十四節氣列入人類非物質文化遺產代表作名錄。
最後一個謎題：如果太陽在六月最高，為什麼台灣最熱的是七、八月？因為海洋和陸地要花好幾週才會熱起來，就像鍋子裡的水，開了爐火還要等一陣子才會沸騰；所以最熱的天氣，會落後最強的陽光一段時間。同樣的延遲，也讓一、二月比十二月更冷。而在南半球，一切都反過來：在澳洲，很多家庭是在海灘上過聖誕節的。
questions: Why can't Earth's distance from the Sun be the cause of the seasons?
What are the two ways that leaning toward the Sun makes the weather warmer?
Why are July and August hotter than June in Taiwan, even though the Sun is highest in June?
answers: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in Taiwan, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons even though they are the same distance from the Sun.
The Sun climbs higher, so its light is concentrated on a smaller area, and the days are longer, so there are more hours of sunlight.
Oceans and land take weeks to warm up, so the warmest weather lags behind the strongest sunlight.

terms.eyebrow: The 24 Solar Terms · 二十四節氣
terms.title_en: A calendar that follows the Sun
terms.lead_en: Each solar term begins when the Sun has moved another 15 degrees along its yearly path. The dates below are calculated for this year, in Taiwan time. Tap any term to see where Earth is on that day.
terms.lead_zh: 太陽每沿著一年的路徑再走 15 度，就進入下一個節氣。下面的日期是今年的日期（台灣時間），當場算出來的；點任何一個節氣，就能看到那天地球在哪裡。

myths.myth_en: Summer is hot because Earth is closer to the Sun.
myths.myth_zh: 夏天熱是因為地球離太陽比較近。
myths.fact_en: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, and its distance changes by only about 3 percent all year. In the model, look for the diamond marked Closest.
myths.fact_zh: 地球在 1 月初離太陽最近，而且整年的距離只差約 3%。在模型裡找找標著「近日點」的菱形。

myths.myth_en: In summer, the noon Sun is straight overhead everywhere.
myths.myth_zh: 夏天的正午，到處都是太陽直射。
myths.fact_en: The Sun can be straight overhead only between the two tropics. Taiwan sits right on the Tropic of Cancer, so its June noon Sun is almost overhead. In Paris, the noon Sun never climbs higher than about 65 degrees.
myths.fact_zh: 只有南北回歸線之間的地方，太陽才可能直射。台灣剛好在北回歸線上，六月正午太陽幾乎在頭頂；在巴黎，正午太陽最高也只到大約 65 度。

myths.myth_en: Earth tips toward the Sun in summer and tips back in winter.
myths.myth_zh: 地球夏天往太陽傾、冬天再倒回來。
myths.fact_en: The axis does not move. It points at the North Star all year. What changes is where Earth is in its orbit, so the same tilt faces toward the Sun in June and away from it in December.
myths.fact_zh: 地軸根本沒有動，整年都指向北極星。改變的是地球在軌道上的位置：同一個傾斜，六月朝向太陽、十二月背向太陽。

myths.myth_en: On the equinox, day and night are exactly 12 hours each.
myths.myth_zh: 春分、秋分那天，白天和黑夜剛好各 12 小時。
myths.fact_en: Almost, but not quite. The air bends sunlight over the horizon, and the Sun is a disk rather than a point, so in Changhua the equinox day lasts about 12 hours and 7 minutes.
myths.fact_zh: 差一點點。大氣會把地平線下的陽光折上來，太陽又是一個圓盤而不是一個點，所以彰化在春分、秋分的白天大約是 12 小時 7 分。

tricks.body_en: If distance caused the seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. They never do.
tricks.body_zh: 如果是距離造成四季，南北半球應該同時過夏天；但它們從來沒有。

tricks.body_en: Summer brings two gifts at once: stronger sunlight because the Sun is higher, and more of it because the day is longer.
tricks.body_zh: 夏天同時帶來兩樣東西：太陽比較高，陽光比較強；白天比較長，陽光的時間也比較多。

tricks.body_en: In the solar terms, spring begins at Start of Spring in early February, about six weeks before the equinox. That is why the Lunar New Year is also called the Spring Festival.
tricks.body_zh: 在節氣裡，春天從 2 月初的立春就開始了，比春分早了大約六週。這也是為什麼農曆新年又叫「春節」。

tricks.body_en: When Taiwan eats tangyuan on the winter solstice, Sydney is having its longest day of the year. Try switching the place in the model.
tricks.body_zh: 台灣在冬至吃湯圓的時候，雪梨正在過一年中白天最長的一天。在模型裡切換地點試試看。

materials.en: A flashlight
materials.zh: 一支手電筒

materials.en: A sheet of graph paper
materials.zh: 一張方格紙

materials.en: A pencil and a ruler
materials.zh: 鉛筆和尺

steps.en: Hold the flashlight straight above the paper, about 30 centimeters away, and trace the bright circle. This is the noon Sun in summer.
steps.zh: 把手電筒垂直舉在方格紙正上方約 30 公分處，描出亮圈的輪廓——這是夏天正午的太陽。

steps.en: Keep the same distance but tilt the flashlight to a low angle, and trace the bright shape again. This is the Sun in winter.
steps.zh: 保持同樣的距離，但把手電筒斜斜地放低，再描一次亮區——這是冬天的太陽。

steps.en: Count the squares inside each shape. The same light now covers many more squares.
steps.zh: 數一數兩個形狀裡各有幾格：同樣的光，現在蓋住了多得多的格子。

steps.en: Ask: which shape would feel warmer on your hand? Why?
steps.zh: 問問自己：哪一個亮區照在手上會比較熱？為什麼？

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: turn off the room lights so the edges are easy to trace. Compare the result with the Noon sunlight panel in the 3D model.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：把教室的燈關掉，亮區的邊緣比較好描。做完再對照 3D 模型裡的「正午陽光」小畫面。

activities.title_en: Walk a Tilted Earth Around the Lamp
activities.title_zh: 帶著傾斜的地球繞燈走一圈

materials.en: A lamp with the shade removed (the Sun)
materials.zh: 一盞拿掉燈罩的檯燈（太陽）

materials.en: A ball with a pencil pushed through it (Earth and its axis)
materials.zh: 一顆插著鉛筆的球（地球與地軸）

materials.en: A sticker to mark Taiwan
materials.zh: 一張標示台灣的小貼紙

steps.en: Put the sticker about a quarter of the way from the equator to the top of the ball.
steps.zh: 把貼紙貼在球上赤道到頂端大約四分之一的位置——這是台灣。

steps.en: Tilt the pencil a little and point its top at one wall of the room. That wall is the North Star.
steps.zh: 把鉛筆稍微傾斜，讓頂端指向教室的某一面牆——那面牆就是北極星。

steps.en: Walk slowly in a circle around the lamp, always keeping the pencil pointed at the same wall.
steps.zh: 繞著檯燈慢慢走一圈，鉛筆的頂端始終指向同一面牆。

steps.en: Stop at four places. Where does the top half of the ball get the most light? Where does it get the least?
steps.zh: 在四個地方停下來看：球的上半部在哪裡被照得最多？在哪裡最少？

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: the most common mistake is turning the pencil to face the lamp. Keeping it pointed at the same wall is the whole point, and exactly what the real axis does.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：最常見的錯誤是把鉛筆轉去朝向檯燈。讓它始終指向同一面牆，正是整個活動的重點，也正是真實地軸的行為。

lessons.title: How Does the Moon Make the Tides?
lessons.blurb_en: Two bulges, two tides a day, and why new and full moons bring the biggest tides, on a real-time 3D Earth.
lessons.blurb_zh: 兩個鼓起、一天兩次滿潮，以及為什麼新月和滿月會漲大潮；3D 地球照真實時間運轉。
lessons.big_idea_en: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder than the far side, stretching the oceans into two bulges. Earth spins through them, so most coasts get two high tides a day.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 月亮對地球近側的拉力比遠側大，把海水拉出兩個鼓起；地球自轉穿過這兩個鼓起，所以大多數海岸一天有兩次滿潮。

lab.title_en: The Oceans on a Stretched Earth
lab.how_en: The blue shell is the ocean, stretched toward and away from the Moon. Press Play at 1 hour a second to watch Taiwan spin through both bulges, or at 2 days a second to watch the Sun and Moon line up for spring tides and pull apart for neap tides. Turn off the Sun's tide to see the Moon working alone.
lab.how_zh: 藍色的殼是海水，被拉向月亮、也被拉向相反的一側。以「每秒 1 小時」播放，看台灣怎麼轉過兩個鼓起；以「每秒 2 天」播放，看日月排成一線時的大潮、互相垂直時的小潮。關掉「太陽的潮汐」，看月亮單獨的作用。

legend.en: Blue shell: the ocean, with its tidal bulges drawn about a million times too tall
legend.zh: 藍色殼：海水；潮汐鼓起放大了約一百萬倍

legend.en: Gold arrows: the tidal force, outward toward and away from the Moon, inward at the sides
legend.zh: 金色箭頭：潮汐力，朝月亮與背向月亮向外、兩側向內

legend.en: Red dot: Changhua, turning with Earth
legend.zh: 紅點：彰化，跟著地球自轉

lab.scale_en: Not to scale. The real tidal bulge in the open ocean is only about half a meter high, on a planet 12,700 km wide, so here it is exaggerated about a million times. The Moon is also drawn much too close and too big. The dates, the positions of the Sun and Moon, and Earth's spin are real.
lab.scale_zh: 未按比例：大洋中真實的潮汐鼓起只有約半公尺，而地球直徑有 12,700 公里，所以這裡放大了大約一百萬倍；月亮也畫得太近、太大。日期、日月的位置與地球自轉都是真實的。

paras: On the coast of Fangyuan in Changhua, farmers drive oxcarts out across the mudflats to tend their oyster beds, and a few hours later the same ground lies under the sea. Twice a day, almost everywhere on Earth, the ocean climbs up the shore and then pulls back again. These tides are so regular that they can be predicted years ahead. Nearly two thousand years ago, the Chinese thinker Wang Chong wrote that the rise of the tides follows the Moon. He was right.

The Moon's gravity pulls on every part of Earth, but not equally. The side of Earth facing the Moon is about 12,700 kilometers closer to it than the far side, so it is pulled a little harder, while the far side is pulled a little less than Earth as a whole. The result is a gentle stretch along the line to the Moon. The oceans, which are free to flow, pile up into two bulges: one on the side facing the Moon and one on the side facing away.

Earth spins once a day underneath these two bulges, so most coasts pass through two high tides and two low tides each day. But the Moon also moves along its orbit, so Earth has to turn a little extra, about 50 minutes, to catch up with it. That is why high tide comes about 50 minutes later each day, just as the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.

The Sun raises tides too. It is far more massive than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times farther away, and the stretching effect weakens very quickly with distance. So the Sun's tides are a little less than half as strong as the Moon's. At new moon and full moon, the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up, the two tides add together, and we get extra-high and extra-low spring tides. The name has nothing to do with the season; it comes from the water springing up. At the first and last quarter, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, partly canceling each other, and the difference between high and low tide is smallest. These are neap tides.

Real coastlines make the picture more complicated. The shape of the sea floor and the coast can funnel the water and make the tides much bigger, or slow them down so that high tide arrives hours after the Moon passes overhead. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water can rise and fall by more than 15 meters. In Taiwan, the tides along the west coast are much larger than on the east coast, which is why the mudflats of Changhua can stretch out for kilometers at low tide.

The tides also have a slow, surprising effect on Earth and the Moon themselves. Water rubbing against the sea floor acts like a brake on Earth's spin, making each day about two thousandths of a second longer every century. In return, the Moon is slowly pushed away, by about 3.8 centimeters a year, which scientists measure by bouncing lasers off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon. Long ago, Earth's pull raised tides in the Moon itself and slowed its spin until one side always faced us. It is the same face we saw in Lesson 1.
paras_zh: 在彰化芳苑的海邊，蚵農駕著牛車穿過泥灘去照顧蚵田；幾個小時後，同一片土地就沉到了海面下。地球上幾乎每個地方，海水一天兩次爬上岸邊、再退回去。潮汐規律到可以提前好幾年預測。將近兩千年前，中國思想家王充就寫下潮水的漲落跟著月亮走——他說對了。
月亮的引力拉著地球的每一個部分，但拉得並不平均。地球面向月亮的一側，比背向的一側離月亮近了大約 12,700 公里，所以被拉得稍微用力一點；而遠側受到的拉力，則比整個地球平均的拉力小一點。結果就是沿著地月連線，地球被輕輕地拉長了。可以自由流動的海水因此堆成兩個鼓起：一個在面向月亮的一側，一個在背向月亮的一側。
地球每天在這兩個鼓起底下自轉一圈，所以大多數海岸每天會經過兩次滿潮、兩次乾潮。但月亮同時也沿著軌道往前走，地球得多轉一點點——大約 50 分鐘——才追得上它。這就是為什麼滿潮每天晚大約 50 分鐘，就像月亮每天晚大約 50 分鐘升起一樣。

太陽也會引起潮汐。它的質量比月亮大得多，但距離也遠了約 400 倍，而這種拉長的效果會隨距離快速減弱，所以太陽的潮汐還不到月亮的一半。在新月和滿月時，太陽、地球、月亮排成一直線，兩股潮汐相加，就出現特別高、也特別低的大潮（spring tide）。這個英文名字跟春天無關，而是來自海水「湧起」（spring up）。在上弦和下弦時，太陽和月亮互相垂直地拉，部分抵銷，漲退的落差最小，這就是小潮（neap tide）。
真實的海岸讓情況複雜得多。海底與海岸的形狀可以把海水像漏斗一樣匯集起來，讓潮汐變得大得多；也可以讓它慢下來，使滿潮在月亮經過頭頂好幾個小時之後才到。加拿大的芬迪灣，漲退落差可以超過 15 公尺。在台灣，西海岸的潮汐比東海岸大得多，這也是為什麼彰化的泥灘在退潮時可以延伸好幾公里。
潮汐對地球和月亮本身，也有緩慢而驚人的影響。海水摩擦海底，就像在地球的自轉上踩了煞車，讓一天的長度每一百年變長大約千分之二秒。作為回報，月亮被慢慢推遠，每年大約 3.8 公分——科學家是用雷射打到太空人留在月球上的反射鏡來量的。很久以前，地球的引力也在月亮身上引起潮汐，把月亮的自轉拖慢，直到它永遠只有一面朝向我們——就是我們在第一課看到的那一面。
questions: Why are there two tidal bulges instead of just one?
Why does high tide come about 50 minutes later each day?
What is the difference between a spring tide and a neap tide?
answers: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder and the far side less than Earth as a whole, so Earth is stretched along the line to the Moon, and water piles up on both the near side and the far side.
The Moon moves along its orbit while Earth spins, so Earth has to turn about 50 extra minutes each day to face the Moon again.
Spring tides come at new and full moon, when the Sun and Moon line up and their tides add together. Neap tides come at the quarter moons, when they pull at right angles and partly cancel.

myths.myth_en: There is only one bulge, on the side facing the Moon.
myths.myth_zh: 只有一個鼓起，就在面向月亮的那一側。
myths.fact_en: There are two. The far side is pulled less than Earth as a whole, so it is left behind and bulges out too. That is why most coasts get two high tides a day, not one.
myths.fact_zh: 有兩個。遠側受到的拉力比整個地球平均的小，被「留在後面」，也鼓了起來。所以大多數海岸一天有兩次滿潮，不是一次。

myths.myth_en: High tide happens exactly when the Moon is overhead.
myths.myth_zh: 月亮在頭頂正上方時，就是滿潮。
myths.fact_en: Coastlines and the sea floor slow the water down, so high tide often arrives hours later, and the delay is different at every port. Always check a real tide table.
myths.fact_zh: 海岸與海底地形會拖慢海水，滿潮常常晚好幾個小時才到，而且每個港口的延遲都不一樣。一定要查真正的潮汐表。

myths.myth_en: The Moon pulls harder at full moon.
myths.myth_zh: 滿月時月亮拉得比較用力。
myths.fact_en: The Moon's pull has nothing to do with how much of it is lit. Spring tides come at both full and new moon because that is when the Sun and Moon line up. As Lesson 1 showed, the phase is only lighting.
myths.fact_zh: 月亮的拉力跟它亮了多少無關。新月和滿月都有大潮，是因為那時日月排成一直線。第一課說過：月相只是光照的角度。

myths.myth_en: Only the oceans have tides.
myths.myth_zh: 只有海水才有潮汐。
myths.fact_en: The solid ground rises and falls too, by up to a few tens of centimeters twice a day. We cannot feel it because everything around us moves together.
myths.fact_zh: 連堅硬的地面也會一天兩次上下起伏，最多可達幾十公分。我們感覺不到，是因為周圍的一切都一起在動。

tricks.body_en: One bulge faces the Moon and one faces away. Earth turns through both every day, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides.
tricks.body_zh: 一個鼓起朝向月亮，一個背向月亮；地球每天轉過兩個，所以大多數海岸一天有兩次滿潮、兩次乾潮。

tricks.body_en: High tide keeps time with the Moon, not the clock. If high tide is at noon today, expect it around 12:50 tomorrow.
tricks.body_zh: 滿潮跟著月亮走，不跟著時鐘走。今天中午滿潮，明天大約就是 12 點 50 分左右。

tricks.title_en: Big tides at new and full moon
tricks.body_en: Spring tides come around the 1st and 15th of the lunar month; neap tides come around the 8th and 23rd.
tricks.body_zh: 大潮在農曆初一、十五前後；小潮在初八、廿三前後。這正是第一課的月相跟潮汐接上的地方。

tricks.title_en: Safety first on the tidal flats
tricks.body_en: On wide mudflats like Changhua's, the rising tide can come in faster than you can walk and fill channels behind you. Check the official tide forecast, leave well before high tide, and never go alone.
tricks.body_zh: 在彰化這樣廣闊的泥灘上，漲潮可能比人走路還快，還會先灌滿你身後的潮溝。出發前查官方潮汐預報、滿潮前提早離開、絕對不要單獨前往。

steps.en: The three students in the line are the near side, the center, and the far side of Earth. Mark where each one stands.
steps.zh: 排成一列的三位學生，分別是地球的近側、中心和遠側。用膠帶標出每個人的位置。

steps.en: The Moon calls out "Pull!" The near student takes three steps toward the Moon, the center student two, and the far student one.
steps.zh: 月亮喊「拉！」近側的同學朝月亮走三步、中心的同學走兩步、遠側的同學走一步。

steps.en: Now look only from the center student's point of view. The near student has moved one step ahead, and the far student has fallen one step behind.
steps.zh: 現在只從中心同學的角度看：近側同學往前多走了一步，遠側同學則落後了一步。

steps.en: Ask: from the middle, which way did each friend move? Both moved away from you. That is the two bulges.
steps.zh: 問問大家：從中間看，兩位同伴往哪裡移動？都是離你而去——這就是兩個鼓起。

lessons.big_idea_en: At night we look out from the side of Earth that faces away from the Sun. As Earth travels around the Sun, that night side points toward different stars, so each season has its own constellations.

paras: On a winter evening in Taiwan, Orion stands high in the south, with the three stars of his belt in a neat row. Look for him on a summer evening, and he is gone. In his place, the curling tail of Scorpius hangs low over the southern horizon, with the red star Antares at its heart. About 1,300 years ago, the poet Du Fu wrote that friends who never meet are like Shen and Shang, two groups of stars that are never in the sky together. Shen is the Chinese name for Orion's main stars, and Shang is Antares. Why do they take turns like that?

First, the stars never go away. They are in the sky during the day as well, but sunlight scattered by the air makes the daytime sky so bright that it hides them. Night is simply the side of Earth that faces away from the Sun. When your part of the world turns into that side, the glare is gone, and you can finally see out into space. So the stars you see at midnight are the stars in the direction opposite the Sun.

Earth also travels around the Sun, once a year. As it moves along its orbit, the night side points in a slowly changing direction, about one degree a day. In winter, it faces the part of space where Orion is. Six months later, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. Now the night side faces Scorpius, while Orion lies behind the Sun, lost in daylight. The stars have not moved; we have. The constellations along the Sun's yearly path are called the zodiac constellations, and the Sun passes in front of a new one about every month.

You can notice this shift a little every night. A star rises about four minutes earlier each evening. That adds up to about two hours a month, so a star that rises at 11 p.m. this month rises around 9 p.m. next month. After a full year, Earth is back where it started, and the same stars return at the same time of night. That is why farmers in ancient China and Egypt could use the stars as a calendar, telling them when to plant and when to expect the rains or the floods.

Different cultures connected the same stars into different pictures. The constellations astronomers use today come mostly from ancient Greece. Ancient Chinese astronomers divided the sky into the Three Enclosures around the North Pole and the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions along the path of the Moon. The two stars in the story of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, Altair and Vega, sit on either side of the Milky Way, the "Silver River." They shine high overhead on summer evenings, around the time of the Qixi Festival on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month.

A constellation is a pattern, not a family. Its stars only look close together because they lie in the same direction. Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder, is roughly 550 to 700 light-years away, while Rigel, his bright foot, is about 860 light-years away. The light you see from Betelgeuse tonight left it at least 500 years ago, during the Ming dynasty or even earlier. Stars do drift, but so slowly that the constellations will look the same for your whole life. So step outside tonight and look up: the sky you see belongs to this season.
paras_zh: 在台灣的冬夜，獵戶座高掛在南方天空，腰帶上的三顆星排得整整齊齊。到了夏天的晚上再去找他，他卻不見了；取而代之的，是天蠍座彎彎的尾巴低掛在南方地平線上，紅色的心宿二就在牠的心臟位置。大約 1,300 年前，詩人杜甫寫道：朋友難得相見，就像天上的參與商，從來不會同時出現。「參」是中國對獵戶座主要亮星的稱呼，「商」就是心宿二。它們為什麼要這樣輪流登場？
首先，星星從來沒有消失。白天它們一樣在天上，只是陽光被空氣散射，讓白天的天空亮得把星星都蓋住了。所謂夜晚，就是地球背對太陽的那一側。當你住的地方轉到這一側，刺眼的陽光不見了，你終於能看進太空。所以午夜看到的星星，就是太陽對面方向的星星。
地球同時也繞著太陽轉，一年一圈。它沿著軌道前進時，夜側指的方向也慢慢改變，大約一天一度。冬天，夜側對著獵戶座所在的那片太空；半年後，地球跑到太陽的另一邊，夜側改對著天蠍座，而獵戶座則躲到太陽背後，淹沒在白天的陽光裡。星星沒有動，是我們在動。沿著太陽一年路線排列的星座，叫做黃道星座；太陽大約每個月換到一個新的黃道星座前面。
每天晚上都能察覺到一點點這種移動：同一顆星每晚大約提早四分鐘升起，一個月累積下來大約兩小時。所以這個月晚上 11 點升起的星，下個月大約 9 點就升起了。整整一年後，地球回到原來的位置，同樣的星星又在夜裡同一個時刻回來。這就是為什麼古代中國和埃及的農民能把星星當作曆法，知道什麼時候該播種、什麼時候雨季或洪水要來了。
不同的文化，把同樣的星星連成不同的圖案。今天天文學家使用的星座，大多來自古希臘。中國古代的天文學家則把天空分成北極周圍的「三垣」，以及沿著月亮路線排列的「二十八宿」。牛郎織女故事裡的兩顆星——牛郎星（河鼓二）和織女星——分別在銀河的兩岸。夏天的晚上，它們高掛頭頂，差不多就是農曆七月初七七夕前後。
星座只是一個圖案，不是一家人。星座裡的星看起來靠在一起，只是因為它們在同一個方向上。獵戶座紅色的肩膀參宿四，距離我們大約 550 到 700 光年；他明亮的腳參宿七，則大約 860 光年遠。今晚你看到參宿四的光，至少在 500 年前就出發了——那時還是明朝，甚至更早。星星其實也在移動，但慢到你一輩子看到的星座都不會變樣。所以今晚走到戶外抬頭看吧：你看到的，正是屬於這個季節的星空。

In summer, Earth is on the other side of the Sun, so Orion lies behind the Sun. It is up during the day and lost in the daylight.

vocab.exzh: 暴風雨過後，風向轉變了。

vocab.ex: Mark the test date on your calendar.
vocab.exzh: 把考試日期標在行事曆上。

vocab.exzh: 博物館裡有古羅馬的錢幣。

quiz.q: Why do we see different constellations in different seasons?
options: Earth moves around the Sun, so the night side faces different stars
The stars move around the sky during the year
Clouds cover different stars each season

quiz.q: Where are the stars during the daytime?
options: Still in the sky, hidden by sunlight

quiz.q: About how much earlier does a star rise each night?
In Du Fu's poem, Shen and Shang are...
options: Orion's stars and Antares, never in the sky together
The Big Dipper and the North Star

options: They lie in about the same direction from Earth, even though their distances are very different
They are all the same distance away

skies.note_en: The brightest sky of the year. Find the Winter Triangle: Betelgeuse, Sirius, and Procyon.
skies.note_zh: 一年中最燦爛的星空。找找冬季大三角：參宿四、天狼星、南河三。

skies.note_en: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle: arc to Arcturus, then speed on to Spica.
skies.note_zh: 順著北斗七星斗柄的弧線：先畫到大角星，再一路延伸到角宿一。

skies.note_en: The Summer Triangle is high overhead. Far from city lights, the Milky Way runs from Cygnus down to Sagittarius.
skies.note_zh: 夏季大三角高掛頭頂。遠離城市燈光時，銀河從天鵝座一路流到人馬座。

skies.note_en: A quiet sky with few bright stars. Fomalhaut sits alone in the south, and the Summer Triangle is still setting in the west.
skies.note_zh: 亮星不多的安靜星空。北落師門孤單地掛在南方，夏季大三角還在西邊慢慢落下。

lessons.skies_note_en: These are the skies over Changhua at 9 p.m. The same stars come back earlier in the night as the months go by, so the "summer" stars are also up before dawn in spring.
lessons.skies_note_zh: 以上是彰化晚上九點的星空。隨著月份推進，同樣的星星會在夜裡越來越早出現；所以「夏季」的星星，春天清晨天亮前就看得到。

tonight.lead_en: Calculated in your browser for today at 9 p.m. Hold your fist at arm's length: one fist is about 10 degrees. A very bright "star" that is not on this list is probably a planet.
tonight.lead_zh: 依今天晚上九點，在你的瀏覽器裡現算。手臂伸直握拳：一個拳頭大約是 10 度。如果看到一顆很亮、卻不在清單上的「星」，多半是行星。

culture_cards.title_zh: 同一片星空，不同的故事
culture_cards.lead_en: Turn on Chinese star groups in the 3D model to see the Chinese pictures drawn over the Western ones.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 打開 3D 模型的「中國星官」，就能看到中國星圖疊在西方星座上的樣子。

cards.quote_zh: 人生不相見，動如參與商。——杜甫〈贈衛八處士〉
cards.quote_en: "In life we seldom meet, just like Shen and Shang." (Du Fu, To the Hermit Wei Ba)
cards.body_en: Shen is Orion's main stars, and Shang is Antares in Scorpius. They sit almost opposite each other in the sky, so one is rising about when the other is setting. The Zuo Zhuan, a history more than 2,000 years old, tells of two quarreling brothers who were sent to live far apart, one to watch Shang and the other to watch Shen.
cards.body_zh: 參是獵戶座的主要亮星，商是天蠍座的心宿二。它們在天上幾乎正對面，一個升起時，另一個差不多正要落下。兩千多年前的《左傳》記載，高辛氏的兩個兒子閼伯與實沈天天爭吵，只好被分開：一個去主管商星，一個去主管參星。

cards.en: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
cards.body_en: Altair, the Cowherd, and Vega, the Weaver Girl, sit on either side of the Milky Way. In the legend, magpies build a bridge so they can meet once a year on Qixi. In reality they are about 15 light-years apart, so even a message sent at the speed of light would take 15 years to arrive.
cards.body_zh: 牛郎星（河鼓二）和織女星隔著銀河相望。傳說每年七夕，喜鵲搭起鵲橋讓他們相會。實際上兩顆星相距大約 15 光年，就算用光速傳訊息，也要走 15 年。

cards.body_en: The Moon takes about 27 days to go once around the sky, so Chinese astronomers marked 28 "mansions" where it stays night after night. Seven mansions make each of four animals: the Azure Dragon of the east, the Black Tortoise of the north, the White Tiger of the west, and the Vermilion Bird of the south. Shen belongs to the White Tiger, and Antares is the Dragon's heart.
cards.body_zh: 月亮大約 27 天在天上繞一圈，古人就沿著它的路線劃出 28 個「宿」，像是月亮每晚住宿的地方。每七宿組成一隻神獸：東方青龍、北方玄武、西方白虎、南方朱雀。參宿屬於白虎，心宿二就是青龍的心臟。

cards.en: A Sky Shaped Like an Empire
cards.body_en: Around the North Pole lies the Purple Forbidden Enclosure, the emperor's palace in the sky; Beijing's Forbidden City is named after it. The Supreme Palace Enclosure is the government, and the Heavenly Market Enclosure is a busy marketplace. In all, the traditional Chinese sky has 283 star groups, while astronomers today divide the sky into 88 constellations.
cards.body_zh: 北極周圍是紫微垣，天帝的宮殿，北京的紫禁城就是照它命名；太微垣是朝廷，天市垣是熱鬧的市集。傳統中國星空一共有 283 個星官，而現代天文學把天空分成 88 個星座。

names.note_en: A red supergiant, one of the Shen stars.

names.cn_en: Heart, second star; the Great Fire
names.note_en: "The Fire flows down in the seventh month" in the Book of Songs: it sinks in the west as summer ends.
names.note_zh: 《詩經》「七月流火」：大火星往西沉，天氣就要轉涼。

names.note_en: Across the Milky Way from Vega.
names.note_zh: 在銀河另一岸與織女星相望。

names.note_en: The brightest star at night. Su Shi wrote of drawing his bow to shoot the Wolf.
names.note_zh: 夜空最亮的恆星。蘇軾：「會挽雕弓如滿月，西北望，射天狼。」

names.note_en: The Dragon's horn, first of the 28 mansions.
names.note_zh: 青龍的角，二十八宿的第一宿。

names.note_en: Its handle points east on spring evenings. More in Lesson 6.
names.note_zh: 「斗柄東指，天下皆春」，下一課再細說。

names.note_en: A symbol of long life, low in the south on winter evenings in Taiwan.
names.note_zh: 象徵長壽的南極仙翁；台灣冬夜低掛南方地平線上。

myths.myth_en: The stars disappear during the day.
myths.myth_zh: 白天星星就不見了。
myths.fact_en: They are always there. Sunlight scattered by the air lights up the whole sky and hides them. During a total solar eclipse, when the Sun is covered, bright stars appear in the middle of the day.
myths.fact_zh: 星星一直都在。陽光被空氣散射，照亮整片天空，把星星蓋住了。日全食時太陽被遮住，大白天也看得到亮星。

myths.myth_en: The constellations change with the seasons because the stars move.
myths.myth_zh: 星座隨季節改變，是因為星星在移動。
myths.fact_en: The stars stay put; Earth moves. As it goes around the Sun, our night side faces a different direction. The stars do drift, but so slowly that Orion looks almost exactly the way it did for Du Fu.
myths.fact_zh: 星星沒動，是地球在動：地球繞太陽走，夜側就對著不同方向。星星其實也在移動，只是慢到我們今天看到的獵戶座，跟杜甫當年看到的幾乎一模一樣。

myths.myth_en: The stars in a constellation are close to each other.
myths.myth_zh: 同一個星座的星星彼此靠得很近。
myths.fact_en: They only lie in the same direction. Rigel is about 860 light-years away, but Bellatrix, Orion's other shoulder, is only about 250. Seen from another star, Orion would not look like a hunter at all.
myths.fact_zh: 它們只是在同一個方向上。參宿七大約 860 光年遠，獵戶座的另一個肩膀參宿五卻只有約 250 光年。從別的恆星看過來，獵戶座根本不像個獵人。

myths.myth_en: On your birthday, the Sun is in front of your horoscope sign.
myths.myth_zh: 生日那天，太陽就在你的星座前面。
myths.fact_en: Usually it is not. The horoscope signs were fixed about 2,000 years ago, and Earth's slow wobble has shifted the sky by almost a whole constellation since then. On October 1 the sign is Libra, but the model shows the Sun in front of Virgo. The Sun also passes through Ophiuchus, a 13th constellation that horoscopes leave out.
myths.fact_zh: 通常不是。星座運勢的「星座」是大約兩千年前定下的，地軸緩慢的晃動（歲差）讓天空至今偏移了將近一整個星座。10 月 1 日在運勢上是天秤座，模型裡的太陽卻在室女座前面。太陽還會經過運勢裡沒有的第 13 個星座：蛇夫座。

tricks.title_en: Four minutes a night, two hours a month
tricks.title_zh: 每晚早 4 分鐘，每月早 2 小時
tricks.body_en: A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night. If Orion rises at 11 p.m. tonight, a month from now it will rise around 9 p.m.
tricks.body_zh: 同一顆星每晚大約提早 4 分鐘升起。如果今晚獵戶座 11 點升起，一個月後大約 9 點就升起了。

tricks.body_en: Orion and Scorpius sit almost opposite each other in the sky, so they take turns: the Shen and Shang of Du Fu's poem.
tricks.body_zh: 獵戶座和天蠍座在天上幾乎正對面，只能輪流登場，這就是杜甫詩裡的參與商。

tricks.body_en: Whatever constellation is opposite the Sun is up all night. In early October the Sun is in Virgo, so Pisces, across the sky, is up from dusk to dawn.
tricks.body_zh: 跟太陽正對面的星座整夜可見。十月初太陽在室女座，對面的雙魚座就從黃昏一直掛到天亮。

tricks.title_zh: 三個大三角，一個四邊形
tricks.body_en: Winter: Betelgeuse, Sirius, Procyon. Spring: Arcturus, Spica, Denebola. Summer: Vega, Altair, Deneb. Autumn has a square instead: the Great Square of Pegasus.
tricks.body_zh: 冬：參宿四、天狼星、南河三。春：大角星、角宿一、五帝座一。夏：織女星、牛郎星、天津四。秋天則是一個四邊形：飛馬座大四邊形。

activities.title_zh: 繞著燈走一圈，看見四季星座

materials.en: A lamp without a shade, in the middle of the room (the Sun)
materials.zh: 一盞沒有燈罩的燈，放在教室中央（太陽）

materials.en: Four paper signs: Pegasus, Orion, Leo, Scorpius
materials.zh: 四張紙牌：飛馬座、獵戶座、獅子座、天蠍座

materials.en: Tape to put the signs on the four walls
materials.zh: 膠帶，把紙牌貼在四面牆上

steps.en: Tape the signs on the four walls, going counterclockwise around the room: Pegasus, Orion, Leo, Scorpius.
steps.zh: 把四張紙牌依逆時針方向貼在四面牆上：飛馬座、獵戶座、獅子座、天蠍座。

steps.en: One student is Earth. Stand between the lamp and the Orion wall, with your back to the lamp. Your face is on the night side. Which constellation do you see? It is winter.
steps.zh: 一位同學當地球，站在燈和獵戶座那面牆之間，背對著燈：你的臉就在夜側。你看到哪個星座？這是冬天。

steps.en: Now turn and face the lamp. That is your daytime sky. Scorpius, behind the lamp, is lost in the glare.
steps.zh: 現在轉身面向燈，這是白天的天空。燈後面的天蠍座被強光淹沒，看不到。

steps.en: Walk a quarter of the way around the lamp, counterclockwise, and stop with your back to the lamp again. Name the season and the constellation at each stop: spring and Leo, summer and Scorpius, autumn and Pegasus.
steps.zh: 沿逆時針方向繞燈走四分之一圈，每停一次都背對著燈。說出每一站的季節和星座：春天獅子座、夏天天蠍座、秋天飛馬座。

steps.en: At any stop, turn slowly in place. The sign in front of you rises on one side and sets on the other: that is one night.
steps.zh: 在任何一站原地慢慢轉一圈：眼前的紙牌從一側「升起」、從另一側「落下」，這就是一個晚上。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: afterward, switch the 3D model to Night side and play it at 20 days a second. It is the same walk, with the real stars.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：活動結束後，把 3D 模型切到「看夜側」，用「每秒 20 天」播放，就是同樣的一圈，只是換成真實的星空。

materials.en: A spot with a clear view to the south or west that you can find again
materials.zh: 一個看得到南方或西方天空、下次還找得到的位置

materials.en: The Tonight's Sky list on this page
materials.zh: 本頁的「今晚彰化的星空」清單

materials.en: Paper, a pencil, and a clock
materials.zh: 紙、鉛筆和時鐘

steps.en: At 8:30 p.m., stand at your spot, such as the school gate or a corner of your balcony. Pick one bright star from the Tonight list.
steps.zh: 晚上 8 點半站在你選的位置（例如校門口或陽台一角），從「今晚」清單裡挑一顆亮星。

steps.en: Sketch the star together with rooftops, trees, or poles. Measure its height with your fist at arm's length: one fist is about 10 degrees.
steps.zh: 把這顆星和屋頂、樹、電線桿一起畫下來。手臂伸直用拳頭量它的高度：一個拳頭大約 10 度。

steps.en: Two weeks later, stand in the same spot at exactly the same time and sketch it again.
steps.zh: 兩週後，在同一個位置、同一個時間，再畫一次。

steps.en: Compare the two sketches. The star has moved about a fist and a half toward the west, because it now arrives at each spot about an hour earlier.
steps.zh: 比較兩張圖：這顆星往西移了大約一個半拳頭，因為它現在每到一個位置，都比兩週前早了大約一小時。

steps.en: Predict: where will it be at 8:30 p.m. two months from now? Check your guess with the 3D model.
steps.zh: 預測看看：兩個月後的晚上 8 點半，它會在哪裡？再用 3D 模型驗證你的答案。

activities.tip_en: Safety tip: stargaze with an adult, and never look straight at the Sun. On a cloudy night, the sky chart in the 3D model shows the same view.
activities.tip_zh: 安全提示：觀星要有大人陪同，絕對不要直視太陽。遇到陰天，3D 模型旁的星空圖一樣看得到同樣的景象。

lessons.title: How Do You Find North at Night?
lessons.blurb_en: Find the North Star with the Big Dipper, see why it never moves, and measure your latitude with your fist, from Changhua to the North Pole.
lessons.blurb_zh: 用北斗七星找到北極星，看懂它為什麼不動；再用拳頭量出你的緯度，從彰化一路到北極點。
lessons.big_idea_en: Earth's axis points almost straight at the North Star, so it stays still while the other stars circle around it. Its height above the horizon equals your latitude.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 地軸幾乎正對著北極星，所以它不動，其他星星都繞著它轉；它離地平線的高度，就等於你所在的緯度。

lab.title_en: The Axis, the Star, and Your Latitude
lab.how_en: From space: Earth's axis points at the North Star. At the chosen place, the gold arc between the ground's north and the line to the North Star is exactly the same as the latitude arc at Earth's center. Switch places and watch both change together. Your sky: the whole dome of stars turns around the North Star; stars inside the teal circle never set. The chart on the right shows the view facing north, with star trails from the past three hours.
lab.how_zh: 從太空看：地軸指向北極星。在所選的地點，「地平線上的北方」和「指向北極星的線」之間的金色角，跟地心的緯度角一模一樣大；換個地點，兩個角一起變。你的天空：整片星空繞著北極星轉，青色圈裡的星永不落下。右邊是面向北方的星圖，附上過去三小時的星軌。

legend.en: White line: Earth's axis, pointing less than one degree from the North Star
legend.zh: 白線：地軸，指向離北極星不到一度的地方

legend.en: Green disk: the ground at the chosen place. Red line: north along the ground
legend.zh: 綠色圓盤：所選地點的地面；紅線：地平線上的北方

legend.en: Gold arcs: the North Star's height at the place and the latitude at Earth's center, always the same angle
legend.zh: 金色弧：地點上北極星的高度，與地心的緯度角，永遠一樣大

legend.en: Your sky: stars inside the teal circle never set; stars inside the red circle never rise
legend.zh: 你的天空：青色圈內的星永不落下，紅色圈內的星永不升起

lab.scale_en: Not to scale. Earth is drawn far too big; the real North Star is more than 400 light-years away, so the lines toward it from anywhere on Earth are parallel. The dates, Earth's spin, and the positions and brightness of the stars are real.
lab.scale_zh: 未按比例：地球畫得太大；真實的北極星在 400 多光年外，所以從地球上任何地方看過去的方向都互相平行。日期、地球自轉、星星的位置與亮度都是真實的。

Stars: Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th ed. (Hoffleit & Warren, 1991; public domain), 1,634 stars brighter than magnitude 5. Constellation lines drawn by twrses.org. Planets are not shown.
星表：耶魯亮星星表第五版（公有領域），亮於 5 等的 1,634 顆星。星座連線為本站自繪。圖中不含行星。

paras: Long before phones and GPS, travelers found their way at night with a single star. On a clear night in Changhua, face north and look about two and a half fists above the horizon. There you will find a star that is not especially bright, yet it does something no other star does: it stays in the same place all night, while the rest of the sky slowly turns around it. This is Polaris, the North Star. Confucius once compared a good ruler to the pole star, which stays in its place while all the other stars turn toward it.

Why does it stay still? Earth spins once a day around its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. Follow that axis out into space from the North Pole, and it lands less than one degree from Polaris. Like the hub of a spinning wheel, Polaris barely moves, while the other stars travel in circles around it: small circles close to it, and big circles farther away. Facing north, you see them turn counterclockwise, about 15 degrees, or one and a half fists, every hour.

Here is the most useful fact of all: the height of the North Star above your horizon equals your latitude. At the North Pole, latitude 90 degrees, Polaris is straight overhead. At the equator, latitude 0, it sits right on the horizon. In Changhua, about 24 degrees north, it is about 24 degrees up. The reason is the curve of Earth: as you travel north, your horizon tilts, and the North Star climbs higher. Sailors used this for centuries. The navigators of Zheng He's fleet measured the North Star's height with wooden boards, in units they called "fingers," to know how far north their ships had sailed.

Polaris is not the brightest star in the sky; dozens of stars outshine it. The easy way to find it is with the Big Dipper, seven bright stars shaped like a ladle. The two stars at the end of the bowl are the Pointers: draw a line through them and go about five times the distance between them, and you arrive at Polaris. In Taiwan, the Big Dipper sinks below the northern horizon on autumn and winter evenings. Then use Cassiopeia, a bright W on the other side of Polaris. The North Star sits about halfway between the two.

The Big Dipper is also a clock and a calendar. It swings around Polaris once a day, and it sits a little farther around at the same hour each night as the seasons change. An old Chinese saying tells where its handle points in the early evening: east in spring, south in summer, west in autumn, and north in winter. From Changhua, the winter position is below the horizon, because at our latitude the Big Dipper sets for part of each night. The 3D model lets you test the saying on any date.

The North Star has not always been the North Star. Earth's axis wobbles slowly, like a spinning top, and traces a big circle in the sky every 26,000 years. When the pyramids of Egypt were built, the pole star was Thuban, in the constellation Draco. In Confucius's time, Polaris was about 15 degrees from the pole, so the pole star he admired was a different star. Polaris will come closest to the pole around the year 2100, and in about 12,000 years bright Vega will take its turn. South of the equator, Polaris drops out of sight, and people use the Southern Cross to find south instead.
paras_zh: 在手機和衛星定位出現之前很久，旅人靠一顆星在夜裡找路。晴朗的晚上在彰化，面向北方，抬頭看地平線上方大約兩個半拳頭高的地方，會找到一顆不怎麼亮的星。它卻做到了別的星星做不到的事：整晚待在同一個位置，其他的星空則慢慢繞著它轉。這就是北極星。孔子曾把好的君王比作北辰：它安居其位，眾星都環繞著它。
它為什麼不動？地球每天繞著地軸自轉一圈，地軸是一條穿過南北極的假想線。從北極沿著地軸往太空延伸，會落在離北極星不到一度的地方。北極星就像旋轉車輪的軸心，幾乎不動；其他星星則繞著它畫圓：離它近的畫小圓，離它遠的畫大圓。面向北方時，會看到它們逆時針轉動，每小時大約 15 度，也就是一個半拳頭。
最有用的一件事是：北極星離地平線的高度，等於你所在的緯度。在北極點（緯度 90 度），北極星就在頭頂正上方；在赤道（緯度 0 度），它貼在地平線上；在彰化（北緯約 24 度），它大約高 24 度。原因是地球是圓的：你往北走，你的地平面跟著傾斜，北極星就爬得越高。水手們用這個方法用了好幾百年。鄭和船隊的領航員拿著木板量北極星的高度，單位叫做「指」，藉此知道船往北航行了多遠。
北極星並不是天上最亮的星，比它亮的星有好幾十顆。要找它，最簡單的方法是用北斗七星——七顆排成長柄勺形狀的亮星。斗杓末端的兩顆星叫「指極星」：把它們連成一線，往外延長大約兩星距離的五倍，就到北極星了。在台灣，秋冬的晚上北斗七星會沉到北方地平線下；這時改用仙后座——北極星另一邊那個明亮的 W。北極星大約就在兩者的中間。
北斗七星也是時鐘和日曆。它每天繞北極星轉一圈，而且隨著季節推移，每晚同一個時刻都會多轉一點點。中國古話說傍晚時斗柄的方向：春天指東、夏天指南、秋天指西、冬天指北。從彰化看，冬天那個位置在地平線下，因為在我們的緯度，北斗七星每晚都有一段時間會落下。3D 模型可以讓你在任何日期驗證這句話。
北極星並不是一直都當北極星。地軸像陀螺一樣緩慢地晃動，每 26,000 年在天上畫一個大圓。埃及建金字塔的時候，北極星是天龍座的右樞（Thuban）。孔子的時代，今天的北極星離天極大約 15 度，所以他讚嘆的北辰是另一顆星。北極星大約在 2100 年最接近天極；再過大約 12,000 年，明亮的織女星就會接班。到了赤道以南，北極星沉到地平線下看不到，人們改用南十字座找南方。
questions: Why does the North Star stay in the same place all night?
How high is the North Star above the horizon in Changhua, and why?
How can you find the North Star when the Big Dipper is below the horizon?
answers: Earth's axis points almost straight at it, so as Earth spins, the North Star barely moves while the other stars circle around it.
About 24 degrees, because the North Star's height equals your latitude, and Changhua is about 24 degrees north.
Use Cassiopeia, the W on the other side of the North Star. Polaris sits about halfway between the W and the Big Dipper.

The North Star pulls them around
The stars orbit the North Star

dipper.note_en: The Dipper climbs high in the northeast with its handle to the east. This is the best season to see the whole shape from Taiwan.
dipper.note_zh: 北斗七星爬上東北方高空，斗柄朝東。在台灣，這是看清整個北斗的最好季節。

dipper.note_en: The Dipper hangs high in the northwest, its handle pointing up toward the south. Follow the curve of the handle to orange Arcturus.
dipper.note_zh: 北斗七星高掛西北方，斗柄往上指向南方。順著斗柄的弧線，就能找到橙色的大角星。

dipper.note_en: The Dipper lies low in the northwest with its handle to the west, and slips below the horizon soon after. Cassiopeia's W takes over.
dipper.note_zh: 北斗七星低低地躺在西北方，斗柄朝西，不久就沉到地平線下；換仙后座的 W 接班。

dipper.note_en: In Changhua the handle, pointing down toward the north, is below the horizon at this hour. Far to the north, in Tromsø, the Dipper never sets.
dipper.note_zh: 在彰化，這個時刻朝下指北的斗柄在地平線下；到了遙遠的特羅姆瑟，北斗七星永遠不會落下。

lessons.dipper_note_en: An old Chinese book, the Heguanzi, says: when the handle points east, it is spring everywhere; south, summer; west, autumn; north, winter. It describes early evening. The cards show 8 p.m. in Changhua.
lessons.dipper_note_zh: 《鶡冠子》：「斗柄東指，天下皆春；斗柄南指，天下皆夏；斗柄西指，天下皆秋；斗柄北指，天下皆冬。」說的是黃昏時的方向；卡片是彰化晚上八點的樣子。

places.title_en: Your Latitude Is Written in the Sky
places.lead_en: The North Star's height equals your latitude, so this table is also a list of latitudes. One fist at arm's length is about 10 degrees.
places.lead_zh: 北極星的高度等於緯度，所以這張表同時也是一張緯度表。手臂伸直握拳，一個拳頭大約 10 度。
places.table_en: How high is the North Star?

rows.note_en: Low in the north. The Big Dipper sets for part of every night.
rows.note_zh: 低掛北方；北斗七星每晚都有一段時間會落下。

rows.note_en: Almost the same as Changhua: all of Taiwan is between 22° and 25°.
rows.note_zh: 和彰化幾乎一樣：整個台灣都在北緯 22° 到 25° 之間。

rows.note_en: Far enough south that the Southern Cross peeks above the sea on spring nights.
rows.note_zh: 夠南，春天夜裡南十字座會從海面上露出來。

rows.note_en: Almost never seen; haze near the horizon hides it.
rows.note_zh: 幾乎看不到，地平線附近的霧氣會把它遮住。

rows.note_en: Higher than in Taiwan; the Big Dipper still sets briefly.
rows.note_zh: 比台灣高；北斗七星仍會短暫落下。

rows.note_en: The Big Dipper never sets here; it circles the North Star all night.
rows.note_zh: 北斗七星在這裡永不落下，整晚繞著北極星轉。

rows.note_en: High in the sky. Cassiopeia and the Dipper wheel around it without setting.
rows.note_zh: 高高在上；仙后座和北斗七星繞著它轉，從不落下。

rows.note_en: Every star circles level with the horizon; nothing rises or sets.
rows.note_zh: 每顆星都和地平線平行地繞圈，不升也不落。

rows.note_en: No North Star at all. Use the Southern Cross to find south.
rows.note_zh: 完全看不到北極星，改用南十字座找南方。

tonight.lead_en: Calculated in your browser for 8 p.m. today. Find a spot with a dark view to the north, away from streetlights, and give your eyes ten minutes to adjust.
tonight.lead_zh: 依今天晚上八點，在你的瀏覽器裡現算。找一個北方沒有路燈、看得到低空的地方，讓眼睛適應黑暗十分鐘。

culture_cards.lead_en: People everywhere have used the still point of the northern sky to rule, to farm, and to find their way.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 世界各地的人，都拿北方天空那個不動的點來治國、務農與認路。

cards.en: A Ruler Like the Pole Star
cards.quote_zh: 為政以德，譬如北辰，居其所而眾星共之。——《論語·為政》
cards.quote_en: "Govern by virtue, like the pole star, which stays in its place while all the other stars turn toward it." (The Analects)
cards.body_en: Confucius saw the pole as the still center of the turning sky, the way a good ruler steadies a country. In his day Polaris was about 15 degrees from the pole, so the star he meant was a different one. The idea has outlasted the star.
cards.body_zh: 孔子把天極看成旋轉星空中不動的中心，就像好的君王穩住一個國家。他那個時代，今天的北極星離天極約 15 度，所以他說的北辰是另一顆星——星星換了，這個道理還在。

cards.body_en: The Heguanzi, a book more than 2,000 years old, tells the seasons by where the Dipper's handle points at dusk. The seven stars have Chinese names too: Tianshu, Tianxuan, Tianji, Tianquan, Yuheng, Kaiyang, and Yaoguang. The first two are the Pointers.
cards.body_zh: 兩千多年前的《鶡冠子》用黃昏時斗柄的方向分辨四季。北斗七星各有名字：天樞、天璇、天璣、天權、玉衡、開陽、搖光；天樞、天璇就是指極星。

cards.body_en: Six hundred years ago, the navigators of Zheng He's fleet held wooden boards of different sizes at arm's length and measured the North Star's height in "fingers." Their charts noted how many fingers high it stood at each port. Near the equator, where the North Star sank too low, they measured the Southern Cross, which they called the Lantern Frame Stars.
cards.body_zh: 六百年前，鄭和船隊的領航員把大小不同的木板伸直手臂舉起，用「指」量北極星的高度；航海圖上記著每個港口北極星有幾指高。到了赤道附近北極星太低，他們就改量南十字座，當時叫「燈籠骨星」。

cards.body_en: A well-known American folk song, "Follow the Drinking Gourd," tells of people escaping slavery who followed the Big Dipper north toward freedom. Anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere, the Dipper leads to the North Star.
cards.body_zh: 美國有一首很有名的民謠〈跟著飲水葫蘆走〉，唱的是逃離奴隸制度的人，跟著北斗七星（飲水葫蘆）一路往北走向自由。在北半球任何地方，北斗七星都能帶你找到北極星。

myths.myth_en: The North Star is the brightest star in the sky.
myths.myth_zh: 北極星是天上最亮的星。
myths.fact_en: Not even close. Dozens of stars are brighter, and Sirius is the brightest of all. Polaris is special because of where it is, not how bright it is.
myths.fact_zh: 差得遠。比它亮的星有好幾十顆，最亮的是天狼星。北極星特別，是因為它的位置，不是因為它的亮度。

myths.myth_en: The North Star is high overhead.
myths.myth_zh: 北極星在頭頂正上方。
myths.fact_en: Only at the North Pole. Its height equals your latitude, so in Changhua it is only about 24 degrees up, two and a half fists. Look low in the north, not straight up.
myths.fact_zh: 只有在北極點才是。它的高度等於緯度，所以在彰化只有大約 24 度高，兩個半拳頭。要往北方低空找，不是往頭頂看。

myths.myth_en: You can see the North Star from anywhere on Earth.
myths.myth_zh: 地球上任何地方都看得到北極星。
myths.fact_en: South of the equator it is below the horizon. People in Australia, South Africa, or Argentina use the Southern Cross to find south instead.
myths.fact_zh: 赤道以南它在地平線下。澳洲、南非、阿根廷的人改用南十字座找南方。

myths.myth_en: The North Star never moves and has always been the North Star.
myths.myth_zh: 北極星完全不動，而且永遠都是北極星。
myths.fact_en: It circles the pole in a tiny ring about as wide as two and a half full Moons. Over thousands of years, Earth's wobble changes which star is near the pole: Thuban for the pyramid builders, Vega in about 12,000 years.
myths.fact_zh: 它其實繞著天極畫一個小圈，寬度大約是兩個半滿月。幾千年下來，地軸的晃動會換掉靠近天極的星：建金字塔時是右樞，大約一萬兩千年後是織女星。

tricks.body_en: Measure the North Star's height and you know how far north you are. Changhua: about 24 degrees, two and a half fists.
tricks.body_zh: 量出北極星的高度，就知道自己在北緯幾度。彰化：大約 24 度，兩個半拳頭。

tricks.body_en: From Merak through Dubhe, the two stars at the end of the Dipper's bowl, go about five times their distance to reach Polaris.
tricks.body_zh: 從天璇經過天樞（斗杓末端的兩顆星），往外延長約五倍的距離，就到北極星。

tricks.title_en: Between the Dipper and the W
tricks.title_zh: 北斗與 W 的正中間
tricks.body_en: Polaris sits about halfway between the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia. When one is low, the other is high.
tricks.body_zh: 北極星大約在北斗七星和仙后座中間；一個低的時候，另一個就高。

tricks.title_en: Counterclockwise, a fist and a half an hour
tricks.title_zh: 逆時針，一小時一個半拳頭
tricks.body_en: Facing north, the stars turn counterclockwise around Polaris, 15 degrees an hour. In six hours the Big Dipper turns a quarter of the way around.
tricks.body_zh: 面向北方，星星繞著北極星逆時針轉，一小時 15 度；六小時後，北斗七星就轉了四分之一圈。

activities.title_en: Measure the North Star with a Protractor

materials.en: A protractor with a small hole at the center of its straight edge
materials.zh: 一個直邊中央有小孔的量角器

materials.en: A drinking straw and some tape
materials.zh: 一根吸管和膠帶

materials.en: A 30-centimeter string with a small weight, such as an eraser or a washer
materials.zh: 一條 30 公分的細繩，綁上小重物（橡皮擦或墊圈）

steps.en: Tape the straw along the straight edge of the protractor.
steps.zh: 把吸管貼在量角器的直邊上。

steps.en: Tie the string through the hole at the center of the straight edge so the weight hangs freely.
steps.zh: 把細繩穿過直邊中央的小孔綁好，讓重物自然垂下。

steps.en: Look through the straw at the top of a flagpole. Pinch the string against the protractor and read where it crosses. The difference between that number and 90 is the height of the flagpole top in degrees.
steps.zh: 透過吸管看旗桿頂端，用手指把細繩按在量角器上，讀出細繩經過的刻度；它和 90 的差，就是旗桿頂端的高度（度）。

steps.en: On a clear night, sight the North Star the same way. You should get about 24 degrees, Changhua's latitude.
steps.zh: 晴朗的晚上用同樣的方法瞄準北極星，應該會量到大約 24 度——正是彰化的緯度。

steps.en: Check with your fist: two and a half fists should match your number.
steps.zh: 再用拳頭驗證：兩個半拳頭應該和你量到的數字差不多。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: this is the same idea as Zheng He's star boards and a sailor's sextant. Collect the whole class's numbers and average them; the average usually lands within a few degrees of 24.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：這和鄭和的牽星板、水手的六分儀是同一個道理。把全班量到的數字平均，通常會落在 24 度上下幾度以內。

materials.en: A plain, dark umbrella
materials.zh: 一把素色的深色雨傘

materials.en: White stickers or chalk
materials.zh: 白色貼紙或粉筆

materials.en: The facing-north chart in the 3D model
materials.zh: 3D 模型旁「面向北方」的星圖

steps.en: Open the umbrella. The center, where the tip is, stands for the North Star.
steps.zh: 打開雨傘，傘尖所在的中心點代表北極星。

steps.en: On the inside of the umbrella, stick the seven stars of the Big Dipper on one side of the center and the W of Cassiopeia on the opposite side.
steps.zh: 在傘的內側，把北斗七星貼在中心的一邊，仙后座的 W 貼在正對面。

steps.en: Face north and hold the umbrella over your head so the tip points about 24 degrees above the northern horizon, toward the real North Star.
steps.zh: 面向北方，把傘舉在頭上，讓傘尖指向北方地平線上方約 24 度，也就是真正的北極星方向。

steps.en: Turn the umbrella slowly counterclockwise. The Dipper and the W take turns rising high and dipping toward the ground, and the center never moves.
steps.zh: 把傘慢慢逆時針轉：北斗和 W 輪流升高、又輪流低到接近地面，只有中心點不動。

steps.en: Tip the umbrella straight up: now you are at the North Pole, and nothing sets. Tip it down to the horizon: now you are at the equator.
steps.zh: 把傘尖轉到正上方：你到了北極點，什麼都不會落下。把傘尖放低到地平線：你到了赤道。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: afterward, open the Your sky view in the 3D model and switch from Changhua to Tromsø and the North Pole. The teal "never sets" circle grows exactly as the umbrella showed.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：做完後打開 3D 模型的「你的天空」，把地點從彰化切到特羅姆瑟、北極點，會看到青色的「永不落下」圈正像雨傘演示的一樣越變越大。

lessons.title: Why Do Planets Wander Across the Sky?
lessons.title_zh: 行星為什麼會在星空中遊走？
lessons.blurb_en: Watch Earth overtake Mars on real orbits, see why planets loop backward among the stars, and find tonight's planets over Changhua.
lessons.blurb_zh: 在真實軌道上看地球超車火星，看懂行星為什麼會在星空中倒退繞圈；再看今晚彰化的天上有哪些行星。
lessons.big_idea_en: Planets go around the Sun at different speeds. When Earth overtakes a slower outer planet, the planet seems to drift backward among the stars for a while.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 行星繞太陽的速度各不相同。地球超車外側較慢的行星時，那顆行星看起來會在星空中倒退一陣子。

lab.how_en: The orbits are real and to scale, and the planets move on real dates. The white sight line runs from Earth through the planet and on to the distant stars. Press Play and watch Earth, on the faster inside track, catch up with Mars and pass it. Around that moment, the planet's path among the stars, on the right, turns orange and runs backward. The numbers 1 to 9 mark the same nine dates in both pictures: Earth and the planet in the 3D model, and the planet's place among the stars on the chart, where the order goes forward, backward, and forward again.
lab.how_zh: 軌道是真實比例，行星照真實日期運行。白色視線從地球穿過行星，一路延伸到遙遠的星空。按下播放，看跑在內圈、速度較快的地球追上火星、超過它；就在超車前後，右邊行星在星空中的路徑變成橘色、往回倒退。1 到 9 的號碼在兩張圖裡標的是同樣九個日期：3D 模型裡是地球和行星的位置，右邊路徑圖上是行星在星空中的位置——順序是前進、倒退、再前進。

legend.en: White line: the sight line from Earth through the planet to the stars
legend.zh: 白線：從地球穿過行星、延伸到星空的視線

legend.en: Numbers 1 to 9: Earth and the planet on nine equally spaced dates, joined by sight lines; orange while the planet moves backward
legend.zh: 號碼 1 到 9：九個等間隔日期的地球與行星位置，以視線相連；行星倒退時是橘色

legend.en: Path in the sky: teal while moving east as usual, orange while moving backward
legend.zh: 天上的路徑：照常往東時是青色，倒退時是橘色

legend.en: Dashed gold circle: the ecliptic, the Sun's path. Planets always stay close to it
