paras: The ancient Greeks noticed that five of the brightest "stars" do not stay put. Night after night, they drift slowly through the constellations of the zodiac, and every so often one of them stops, turns around, and moves backward for weeks before going forward again. The Greeks called them planetes, which means "wanderers," and that is where our word planet comes from. Chinese astronomers watched the same lights. They named Mars Yinghuo, "the dazzling puzzler," because its path was so hard to predict.

Today we know that the planets, Earth included, all travel around the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same flat plane. That is why they always appear near the zodiac, along the Sun's yearly path. The closer a planet is to the Sun, the faster it goes. Mercury makes a full lap in 88 days, Earth in a year, Mars in about two years, Jupiter in about 12 years, and Saturn in almost 30. Seen from Earth, a planet usually creeps a little farther east among the stars each night.

So why does a planet sometimes go backward? Think of riding in a car on the highway. As you pass a slower truck, the truck seems to slide backward against the faraway mountains, even though it is still moving forward. Earth, on its faster inside track, passes Mars about every 26 months. For a couple of months around that time, Mars appears to drift west against the stars, then turns east again. Astronomers call this retrograde motion. It happens when the planet is on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun, so the planet is also at its closest, brightest, and up all night.

Explaining these loops took a very long time. About 1,900 years ago, the astronomer Ptolemy put Earth at the center and moved each planet on small circles riding on bigger circles. His system worked well enough to predict the planets, but it was complicated. In 1543, Copernicus put the Sun at the center instead, and the loops suddenly made simple sense: they are just what you see when a moving Earth overtakes another planet. Retrograde motion became one of the strongest clues that Earth itself is moving.

In Chinese, the five planets you can see with the naked eye are named after the five elements: Mercury is the water star, Venus the metal star, Mars the fire star, Jupiter the wood star, and Saturn the earth star. Their older names describe how they behave. Jupiter was the "year star," because it moves about one twelfth of the way around the sky each year, and people used it to count years. Venus was called Qiming, the morning star, when it rose before dawn, and Changgeng, the evening star, when it shone after sunset.

You do not need a telescope to find a planet. Look near the zodiac for a bright point that shines with a steady light, because stars twinkle more than planets do. Venus is the brightest thing in the night sky after the Moon, and Jupiter comes next. A planet will not stay among the same stars for long, so it never appears on the star maps from Lesson 5. Check the list of tonight's planets below, then look up and watch a wanderer move from one week to the next.
paras_zh: 古希臘人注意到，天上最亮的「星」裡有五顆不肯待在原地。它們一夜接一夜，慢慢穿過黃道上的星座；每隔一陣子，其中一顆會停下來、掉頭，往回走好幾個星期，然後才再往前。希臘人叫它們 planetes，意思是「漫遊者」，英文的 planet（行星）就是這麼來的。中國的天文學家看著同樣的光點，把火星叫做「熒惑」——閃閃發光、又讓人困惑，因為它的路線實在太難預測了。
今天我們知道，包括地球在內，所有行星都以同一個方向、在幾乎同一個平面上繞著太陽轉。所以行星總是出現在黃道附近，也就是太陽一年走過的路線上。離太陽越近的行星跑得越快：水星 88 天繞一圈，地球一年，火星大約兩年，木星大約 12 年，土星將近 30 年。從地球看，行星通常每天晚上在星空中往東多挪一點點。
那行星為什麼有時候會倒退？想像你坐在高速公路上的車裡。超過一輛比較慢的卡車時，卡車好像在遠方山景前面往後滑，雖然它其實還在往前開。地球跑在比較快的內圈，大約每 26 個月超車火星一次。超車前後的兩個月左右，火星看起來在星空中往西倒退，然後才轉回往東。天文學家把這叫做「逆行」。逆行發生在行星位在地球另一邊、正對太陽的時候，所以這時它也離我們最近、最亮，而且整夜都看得到。
要解釋這些倒退繞圈，人類花了很久的時間。大約 1,900 年前，天文學家托勒密把地球放在中心，讓每顆行星在「大圓上的小圓」（本輪）上運行。他的系統足以預測行星的位置，但非常複雜。1543 年，哥白尼改把太陽放在中心，繞圈一下子就變得簡單：那只是會動的地球超過另一顆行星時看到的景象。逆行因此成了「地球本身在動」最有力的線索之一。
中文裡，肉眼看得到的五顆行星用五行命名：水星、金星、火星、木星、土星。它們更古老的名字描述了它們的行為：木星叫「歲星」，因為它每年大約在天上走十二分之一圈，古人拿它來紀年；金星在日出前升起時叫「啟明」，日落後閃耀時叫「長庚」。
找行星不需要望遠鏡。在黃道附近找一個穩穩發亮的光點，因為恆星比行星更會閃爍。金星是夜空中除了月亮以外最亮的天體，其次是木星。行星不會在同一群星星之間待很久，所以第五課的星圖上從來沒有它們。看看下面今晚的行星清單，然後抬頭，一週一週地看一顆漫遊者怎麼移動。
questions: Why does Mars sometimes seem to move backward among the stars?
Why are planets always found near the zodiac constellations?
How did retrograde motion help show that Earth moves?
answers: Earth, on its faster inside orbit, overtakes Mars. Like a slower truck you pass on the highway, Mars seems to slide backward against the distant stars, even though it is still moving forward.
All the planets go around the Sun in nearly the same flat plane as Earth, so they always appear close to the Sun's path, the zodiac.
Copernicus showed that the loops are simply what you see when a moving Earth overtakes another planet, so the loops became a strong clue that Earth itself is moving.

wanderers.note_en: Always close to the Sun, so look low in the twilight. It goes backward when it passes between Earth and the Sun.
wanderers.note_zh: 總是離太陽很近，要在黃昏或清晨的低空找。它從地球與太陽之間經過時會逆行。

wanderers.note_en: The brightest planet. The morning star (Qiming) or the evening star (Changgeng), but never up at midnight.
wanderers.note_zh: 最亮的行星。清晨叫啟明、黃昏叫長庚，但半夜永遠看不到。

wanderers.note_en: Orange-red, with the biggest backward loop. It is brightest when Earth overtakes it.
wanderers.note_zh: 橘紅色，逆行的圈最大；地球超車它的時候最亮。

wanderers.note_en: Brilliant and creamy white, second only to Venus. It moves about one constellation a year.
wanderers.note_zh: 明亮的乳白色，僅次於金星；大約每年移動一個星座。

wanderers.retro_zh: 每 12 個半月逆行一次
wanderers.note_en: Soft and golden, the slowest wanderer. It spends more than four months of every year going backward.
wanderers.note_zh: 柔和的金黃色，走得最慢的漫遊者；每年有四個多月在逆行。

lessons.wanderers_note_en: The dates below are calculated in your browser, so they are always up to date. Uranus and Neptune are planets too, but they are too faint to see without a telescope.
lessons.wanderers_note_zh: 下面的日期在你的瀏覽器裡現算，永遠是最新的。天王星和海王星也是行星，但太暗了，沒有望遠鏡看不到。

tonight.lead_zh: 依今天的日期在你的瀏覽器裡現算。黃昏的行星以天剛黑時為準，清晨的以天亮前為準，其餘以晚上九點為準。

culture_cards.lead_en: Every culture that watched the sky noticed the five lights that do not stay put, and gave them names that still live in our calendars.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 每個觀察天空的文化，都注意到這五個不肯待在原地的光點，給了它們名字——有些到今天還留在我們的日曆裡。

cards.k: 熒惑守心 · Mars and Antares
cards.en: When Mars Lingers at the Heart
cards.body_en: When Mars slowed down, stopped, and lingered near Antares, the red heart of the Azure Dragon, Chinese court astronomers took it as a grave warning for the emperor. Today we know it is just a retrograde loop near the zodiac. Fittingly, the name Antares means "rival of Mars," because the two are so alike in color.
cards.body_zh: 火星減速、停留、在青龍的紅色心臟心宿二附近徘徊時，古代朝廷的天文官視為對帝王的嚴重警訊，這就是「熒惑守心」。今天我們知道那只是黃道附近的一次逆行繞圈。有趣的是，Antares 這個名字的意思正是「火星的對手」，因為兩者顏色太像了。

cards.body_en: Jupiter takes about 12 years to circle the sky, so it moves through about one twelfth each year. Ancient Chinese astronomers used it to count years, and invented Taisui, an imaginary partner that moves the opposite way, to keep the count tidy. That is the Taisui of the old year-counting customs.
cards.body_zh: 木星大約 12 年在天上繞一圈，每年走大約十二分之一，古人就用它來紀年，稱為「歲星」。為了計算方便，又假想出一顆反方向運行的「太歲」——民間說的「太歲」就是從這裡來的。

cards.k: 啟明與長庚 · Morning and Evening
cards.quote_zh: 東有啟明，西有長庚。——《詩經·小雅·大東》
cards.quote_en: "In the east is Qiming; in the west is Changgeng." (The Book of Songs)
cards.body_en: Long ago, people thought the bright morning star and the bright evening star were two different stars. Both are Venus, which swings from one side of the Sun to the other. The ancient Greeks also had two names for it, Phosphorus and Hesperus, before they realized it was one planet.
cards.body_zh: 很久以前，人們以為清晨的亮星和黃昏的亮星是兩顆不同的星；其實都是金星，它在太陽的兩側來回擺盪。古希臘人也曾給它兩個名字：晨星 Phosphorus 和昏星 Hesperus，後來才發現是同一顆。

cards.k: 星期 · Days of the Week
cards.body_en: The seven-day week was named for the Sun, the Moon, and the five wandering planets. You can still hear them: Saturday is Saturn's day, and in French, Tuesday through Friday are the days of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus. In Japanese, the weekdays are fire, water, wood, metal, and earth, the same planets with their Chinese names.
cards.body_zh: 一週七天原本是用太陽、月亮和五顆行星命名的，現在還聽得出來：英文的 Saturday 是土星日；法文的星期二到星期五是火星、水星、木星、金星的日子；日文的星期是「日月火水木金土」，正是行星的中文名字。

myths.myth_en: During retrograde, a planet really turns around and moves backward.
myths.myth_zh: 逆行的時候，行星真的掉頭往回走。
myths.fact_en: It never does. Every planet keeps going around the Sun in the same direction. The backward drift is only how it looks from a moving Earth, the same way a slower truck seems to slide back as you pass it.
myths.fact_zh: 從來沒有。每顆行星都一直朝同一個方向繞太陽。倒退只是從會動的地球看過去的樣子，就像你超車時，比較慢的卡車看起來往後滑。

myths.myth_en: You need a telescope to see the planets.
myths.myth_zh: 要有望遠鏡才看得到行星。
myths.fact_en: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are all easy to see with the naked eye. People have watched them for thousands of years. A small telescope adds Jupiter's moons and Saturn's rings.
myths.fact_zh: 水星、金星、火星、木星、土星用肉眼都看得到，人類已經看了幾千年。小望遠鏡則能多看到木星的衛星和土星的光環。

myths.myth_en: Planets twinkle just like stars.
myths.myth_zh: 行星和恆星一樣會閃爍。
myths.fact_en: Planets usually shine with a steadier light. A star is so far away that it is a single point, and our moving air makes it flicker. A planet is a tiny disk, so the flickering mostly averages out, except very low in the sky.
myths.fact_zh: 行星的光通常比較穩。恆星遠到只是一個點，流動的空氣讓它忽明忽暗；行星是一個小圓盤，閃爍大多互相抵消了，只有很靠近地平線時才會閃。

myths.myth_en: A planet can show up anywhere in the sky.
myths.myth_zh: 行星可能出現在天空的任何地方。
myths.fact_en: Planets always stay close to the ecliptic, the Sun's path through the zodiac, because all the orbits lie in nearly the same plane. If a bright "star" is far from the zodiac, it is not a planet.
myths.fact_zh: 行星永遠在黃道（太陽穿過黃道星座的路線）附近，因為所有軌道幾乎在同一個平面上。離黃道很遠的亮星，就不是行星。

tricks.body_en: When you pass a slower truck, it seems to slide backward against the mountains. When Earth passes a slower planet, it seems to slide backward against the stars.
tricks.body_zh: 超過慢卡車時，卡車好像在山景前往後滑；地球超過慢的行星時，行星就好像在星空前往後滑。

tricks.body_en: A bright point that does not twinkle, close to the Sun's path, is almost always a planet.
tricks.body_zh: 在黃道附近、不太閃爍的亮點，幾乎一定是行星。

tricks.body_en: An outer planet goes backward when it is opposite the Sun: closest to Earth, at its brightest, and up from dusk to dawn. That is the best time to look.
tricks.body_zh: 外行星逆行時正對太陽：離地球最近、最亮、從黃昏掛到天亮——正是看它的最好時機。

tricks.body_en: Months between backward loops: Mars about 26, Jupiter about 13, Saturn about 12½. The slower the planet, the sooner Earth laps it again.
tricks.body_zh: 兩次逆行相隔幾個月：火星約 26、木星約 13、土星約 12 個半。行星走得越慢，地球越快再超它一圈。

materials.en: Chalk to draw two circles around a center point: a small one for Earth and a bigger one for Mars
materials.zh: 粉筆：繞著中心點畫兩個圓，小圓是地球的軌道，大圓是火星的軌道

materials.en: A long wall or fence beyond the circles, with paper signs numbered 1 to 15 spaced along it as distant stars
materials.zh: 圓圈外的一道長牆或圍欄，貼上編號 1 到 15 的紙卡，當作遙遠的星星

materials.en: Two students, Earth and Mars, plus a recorder with paper
materials.zh: 兩位學生扮地球和火星，一位記錄員拿紙筆

steps.en: Earth and Mars stand on their circles on the same side of the center, Earth a little behind. Both walk counterclockwise; Earth takes two steps for every one step of Mars.
steps.zh: 地球和火星站在各自的圓上、在中心點的同一側，地球稍微落後。兩人都逆時針走，地球每走兩步，火星走一步。

steps.en: Every few steps, the teacher calls "Stop!" Earth points at Mars and keeps pointing past Mars to the wall, and the recorder writes down which numbered sign it hits.
steps.zh: 老師每隔幾步喊「停！」地球伸手指向火星，再一路指到牆上，記錄員寫下指到第幾號紙卡。

steps.en: Keep going until Earth has passed Mars and moved well ahead.
steps.zh: 一直走到地球超過火星、領先一大段為止。

steps.en: Read the list aloud. The numbers climb, then go back down for a while, then climb again: that is retrograde motion.
steps.zh: 把記錄念出來：數字先變大、接著有一陣子變小，然後又變大——這就是逆行。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: then turn on the numbered sight lines in the 3D model. On the path chart, the numbers 1 to 9 follow the same forward, backward, forward order as the class's list.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：接著打開 3D 模型的「編號視線」，右邊路徑圖上 1 到 9 的順序，就和全班記錄的一樣：前進、倒退、前進。

activities.title_en: Track a Planet for a Month

materials.en: The Tonight's Planets list on this page
materials.zh: 本頁的「今晚的行星」清單

materials.en: A printed star chart of that part of the zodiac, or the path chart in the 3D model
materials.zh: 那一段黃道星空的星圖（可以用 3D 模型旁的路徑圖）

materials.en: A pencil
materials.zh: 一支鉛筆

steps.en: Pick a planet that is easy to see this month, such as Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars.
steps.zh: 挑一顆這個月好找的行星，例如木星、土星或火星。

steps.en: Once a week, at the same time of night, find it and mark a dot on your chart next to the stars around it. Write the date beside the dot.
steps.zh: 每週一次、在晚上同一個時刻找到它，在星圖上畫一個點，標出它和旁邊星星的相對位置，並寫上日期。

steps.en: After four or five weeks, connect the dots. Is it moving east (left) or west (right)?
steps.zh: 四、五週後把點連起來：它是往東（左）還是往西（右）走？

steps.en: Compare your drawing with the path chart in the 3D model for the same dates.
steps.zh: 和 3D 模型路徑圖上同一段日期比一比。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: a planet that is in retrograde this month, shown in the Tonight list, gives the most exciting result. Saturn and Jupiter move slowly, so compare them with a bright star right next to them.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：挑「今晚」清單上正在逆行的行星，結果最精采。土星和木星移動得慢，要拿緊鄰的一顆亮星當參考。

lessons.title: How Did People Tell Time by the Sun?
lessons.title_zh: 古人怎麼用太陽看時間？
lessons.blurb_en: Turn a stick into a clock, tilt it toward the North Star to make a sundial, and find out why a Changhua sundial can be 19 minutes off your watch.
lessons.blurb_zh: 把一根竿子變成時鐘，再讓它斜斜指向北極星做成日晷；看看彰化的日晷為什麼會和手錶差到 19 分鐘。
lessons.big_idea_en: As the Sun crosses the sky, a stick's shadow swings around, so a stick can be a clock. But sundial time and clock time drift apart during the year, by up to about 16 minutes.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 太陽橫越天空，竿子的影子就跟著轉，所以一根竿子就能當時鐘。但日晷時間和時鐘時間在一年中會慢慢錯開，最多大約 16 分鐘。

lab.how_en: The Sun moves along its real path over Changhua for the chosen date. With the shadow stick, the white dots mark where the shadow's tip falls at each hour of sundial time; the colored curves show the same tip path on the solstices, so you can see the hour marks move with the seasons. Switch to the sundial: its gnomon points at the North Star, so the shadow turns 15 degrees every hour, all year round. On the right, compare the sundial with the clock, and press 3 days a second to watch the gap open and close through the year.
lab.how_zh: 太陽沿著所選日期在彰化上空的真實路徑移動。看「立竿見影」時，白點是日晷每個整點時影子頂端落下的位置；彩色曲線是冬至、夏至同一條影子頂端的路徑——可以看到整點的位置會隨季節改變。切到「赤道式日晷」：晷針指向北極星，影子一年到頭都是每小時轉 15 度。右邊對照日晷和時鐘；按「每秒 3 天」，看兩者的差距在一年中怎麼拉開、又收回來。

paras: Long before anyone owned a clock, the Sun was the clock. Push a stick straight into the ground on a sunny morning, and its shadow stretches far to the west. As the hours pass, the shadow swings around and shrinks, until around midday it is at its shortest and points due north. Then it grows again toward the east until sunset. An old Chinese saying, "set up a pole and see its shadow," still means getting results right away. With a stick and a few pebbles to mark the shadow, anyone can tell the time.

The shadow moves because Earth spins. Every hour, Earth turns 15 degrees, so the Sun appears to cross the sky from east to west, and the shadow always points away from the Sun. In the morning, when the Sun is low in the east, the shadow is long and points west. At noon, the Sun is highest in the south, and the shadow is shortest. In the evening, the Sun sinks in the west, and the shadow stretches long toward the east.

A plain stick, however, is not a very good clock. As you saw in Lesson 3, the Sun takes a high path in summer and a low path in winter, so the shadow at nine o'clock in June does not land where it lands at nine o'clock in December. The fix is to tilt the stick so that it points at the North Star, parallel to Earth's axis, as you saw in Lesson 6. In Changhua, that means tilting it 24 degrees above the northern horizon. Now the shadow turns evenly, 15 degrees every hour, all year round. This tilted pointer is called the gnomon, and the great equatorial sundial in front of the Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing's Forbidden City works exactly this way.

The shadow's length is a calendar, too. At noon, the shadow is shortest at the summer solstice and longest at the winter solstice. Chinese astronomers measured it for thousands of years with a gnomon called a guibiao: a tall pole with a ruler lying north along the ground. In 1276, Guo Shoujing built one 40 chi tall, five times the usual height, and measured the length of the year as 365.2425 days, the same value our calendar uses today. In Changhua, the noon shadow almost disappears in June, because the Tropic of Cancer passes just to the south, through Chiayi.

If you check a sundial against your watch, you will notice they rarely agree. A clock ticks at the same rate all year, but the Sun does not keep perfect time. Earth's orbit is an oval, so Earth moves faster in January, when it is closest to the Sun, and its tilted axis adds another wobble. Together, they make sundial time run up to about 16 minutes ahead of clock time in early November and about 14 minutes behind in mid-February. Astronomers call this difference the equation of time.

There is one more twist. All of Taiwan sets its clocks by the Sun's position at 120 degrees east, but Changhua lies a little farther east, so its sundials run about 2 minutes ahead. Add it all up, and a Changhua sundial is about 19 minutes fast in early November and about 12 minutes slow in mid-February. Before time zones, every town set its clocks by its own Sun. Railroads in the United States finally adopted standard time zones in 1883, so trains could keep one schedule. On the next sunny day, stand a pencil in the ground and see what time the Sun says it is.
paras_zh: 在大家擁有時鐘之前很久，太陽就是時鐘。晴朗的早晨把一根竿子直直插進地裡，它的影子會遠遠伸向西方。隨著時間過去，影子轉動、縮短，到了中午前後最短，指向正北；然後又往東邊越拉越長，直到日落。中國的成語「立竿見影」，到今天還是指馬上見到成效。只要一根竿子和幾顆小石頭標記影子，誰都能看出時間。
影子會動，是因為地球在自轉。地球每小時轉 15 度，所以太陽看起來從東往西橫越天空，而影子永遠指向背對太陽的方向。早上太陽低低地在東方，影子又長又指向西；中午太陽在南方最高處，影子最短；傍晚太陽在西方落下，影子往東拉得很長。
不過，一根普通的竿子並不是很好的時鐘。第三課說過，太陽夏天走得高、冬天走得低，所以六月早上九點的影子，和十二月早上九點的影子落在不同的地方。解決辦法是把竿子斜過來，讓它指向北極星，也就是和地軸平行——第六課看過的那條線。在彰化，就是斜到北方地平線上方 24 度。這樣影子就會均勻地轉動，一年到頭每小時都是 15 度。這根斜斜的指針叫做「晷針」；北京紫禁城太和殿前的赤道式日晷，就是這樣運作的。
影子的長度也是一本日曆。正午的影子在夏至最短、冬至最長。中國天文學家用一種叫「圭表」的工具量了幾千年：一根高高的「表」，加上一把平躺在地上、指向北方的尺「圭」。1276 年，郭守敬造了一座高 40 尺的高表，是傳統高度的五倍，量出一年是 365.2425 天——和今天全世界使用的曆法一模一樣。在彰化，六月正午的影子幾乎消失，因為北回歸線就在南邊不遠處，穿過嘉義。
如果拿日晷和手錶對時，會發現它們很少一致。時鐘一年到頭走得一樣快，太陽卻不是完美的報時員。地球的軌道是橢圓，一月離太陽最近時走得比較快；傾斜的地軸又再加上一層變化。兩者加起來，讓日晷時間在十一月初比時鐘快將近 16 分鐘，二月中又慢大約 14 分鐘。天文學家把這個差叫做「均時差」。
還有一個轉折。全台灣的時鐘都以東經 120 度的太陽位置為準，但彰化稍微偏東一點，所以彰化的日晷又快了大約 2 分鐘。全部加起來，彰化的日晷在十一月初大約快 19 分鐘，二月中大約慢 12 分鐘。在有時區以前，每個城鎮都照自己的太陽對時；直到 1883 年，美國的鐵路才採用標準時區，讓火車能用同一張時刻表。下一個晴天，把一枝鉛筆插在地上，看看太陽說現在幾點。
questions: Why does a stick's shadow move during the day?
Why should a sundial's gnomon point at the North Star?
Give two reasons a Changhua sundial and a clock can disagree.
answers: Earth spins 15 degrees every hour, so the Sun moves across the sky, and the shadow always points away from the Sun.
Then it is parallel to Earth's axis, so the shadow turns evenly, 15 degrees every hour, in every season.

Earth's oval orbit and tilted axis make the Sun run up to about 16 minutes fast or 14 minutes slow (the equation of time), and Changhua lies east of 120 degrees east, which Taiwan's clocks follow, so its sundials run about 2 minutes ahead.

instruments.meta_en: Tells the hour and the season
instruments.note_en: The simplest sun clock. Its noon shadow is a calendar: shortest at the summer solstice, longest at the winter solstice. But its hour marks shift with the seasons.
instruments.note_zh: 最簡單的太陽時鐘。正午的影子就是日曆：夏至最短、冬至最長。但它的整點位置會隨季節移動。

instruments.meta_zh: 一年到頭每小時 15 度
instruments.note_en: The gnomon points at the North Star and the dial faces the equator. Read the top face from spring to autumn and the bottom face from autumn to spring.
instruments.note_zh: 晷針指向北極星，晷面和赤道平行。春分到秋分看上面，秋分到春分看下面。

instruments.meta_en: Evenly spaced hours, one time zone
instruments.meta_zh: 均勻的鐘點，同一個時區
instruments.note_en: A clock follows an imaginary Sun that moves at a perfectly even pace, set to 120 degrees east for all of Taiwan. The real Sun runs up to 19 minutes ahead in Changhua.
instruments.note_zh: 時鐘跟著一個「假想的、走得完全均勻的太陽」，全台灣都以東經 120 度為準。在彰化，真正的太陽最多會快 19 分鐘。

lessons.instruments_note_en: Each instrument fixes a problem with the one before: the stick tells time roughly, the tilted gnomon makes the hours even, and the clock makes every day the same length.
lessons.instruments_note_zh: 每一種儀器都解決了前一種的問題：竿子能大致看時間，斜放的晷針讓鐘點均勻，時鐘則讓每一天都一樣長。

tonight.lead_en: Calculated in your browser for today. When a sundial in Changhua shows each hour, this is what your clock will say.
tonight.lead_zh: 依今天的日期在你的瀏覽器裡現算：彰化的日晷指到每個整點時，你的時鐘是幾點幾分。

culture_cards.lead_en: Many of the words we use for time were born from shadows and sundials.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 我們談時間的許多說法，都是從影子和日晷來的。

cards.body_en: At Dengfeng in Henan, Guo Shoujing built an observatory with a gnomon 40 chi tall. Its long shadow made noon measurements five times more precise, and his Shoushi calendar of 1281 set the year at 365.2425 days, the same length as the calendar used worldwide today, three centuries earlier.
cards.body_zh: 郭守敬在河南登封建造觀星台，高表達 40 尺。更長的影子讓正午的測量精確了五倍；他 1281 年頒行的《授時曆》把一年定為 365.2425 天，和今天全世界使用的曆法相同，卻早了三百年。

cards.body_en: In front of the Hall of Supreme Harmony stands a stone equatorial sundial, tilted to Beijing's latitude so its gnomon points at the North Star. Its place beside the throne hall showed that the emperor kept heaven's time.
cards.body_zh: 太和殿前立著一座石造赤道式日晷，依北京的緯度傾斜，晷針指向北極星。它擺在大殿旁邊，象徵天子掌握天時。

cards.body_en: The meridian is the north–south line the Sun crosses at noon. A.m. is Latin for "before the meridian," and p.m. means "after the meridian." O'clock is short for "of the clock," once used to tell clock time apart from sundial time.
cards.body_zh: 子午線是太陽正午時經過的南北線。a.m. 是拉丁文「子午線之前」，p.m. 是「子午線之後」。o'clock 是 of the clock（照時鐘的）的縮寫，以前用來區分時鐘時間和日晷時間。

cards.body_en: Before 1883, each American town kept its own sun time, so a railroad might juggle dozens of different noons. On November 18, 1883, the railroads switched to a few standard time zones. Taiwan's zone today is set by 120 degrees east, eight hours ahead of Greenwich.
cards.body_zh: 1883 年以前，美國每個城鎮都用自己的太陽時，一條鐵路可能要應付幾十種不同的「中午」。1883 年 11 月 18 日，鐵路公司改用幾個標準時區。今天台灣的時區以東經 120 度為準，比格林威治快八小時。

myths.myth_en: A sundial always matches the clock.
myths.myth_zh: 日晷和時鐘永遠一致。
myths.fact_en: They agree only on a few days a year. In Changhua, a sundial runs about 19 minutes fast in early November and about 12 minutes slow in mid-February.
myths.fact_zh: 一年只有少數幾天一致。在彰化，日晷十一月初大約快 19 分鐘，二月中大約慢 12 分鐘。

myths.myth_en: At 12 o'clock, the Sun is straight overhead.
myths.myth_zh: 中午 12 點，太陽就在頭頂正上方。
myths.fact_en: Solar noon rarely falls at 12:00 by the clock, and the Sun is straight overhead only between the tropics. In Changhua, the noon Sun is always at least a little to the south.
myths.fact_zh: 太陽正午很少剛好在時鐘的 12:00，而且只有在南北回歸線之間，太陽才會到正頭頂。在彰化，正午的太陽永遠至少稍微偏南。

myths.myth_en: Noon shadows always point north.
myths.myth_zh: 正午的影子永遠朝北。
myths.fact_en: Not south of the Tropic of Cancer. In Tainan and Kaohsiung, the noon Sun passes overhead twice a year, and for a few weeks around June the noon shadow points south. In Changhua, just north of the line, it always points north.
myths.fact_zh: 在北回歸線以南就不是。台南、高雄每年有兩次太陽正午到頭頂，六月前後有幾個星期，正午的影子朝南。彰化在北回歸線稍北，影子永遠朝北。

myths.myth_en: A sundial works the same anywhere you put it.
myths.myth_zh: 日晷放在哪裡都一樣準。
myths.fact_en: A sundial is built for one latitude: its gnomon must tilt at that latitude and point to true north, not magnetic north. A Changhua sundial tilts 24 degrees; one in Boston tilts 42.
myths.fact_zh: 日晷是為某個緯度做的：晷針要依當地緯度傾斜，並指向真北（不是羅盤的磁北）。彰化的日晷斜 24 度，波士頓的要斜 42 度。

tricks.title_en: The gnomon points at the North Star
tricks.body_en: Tilt the pointer to your latitude, 24 degrees in Changhua, so it lies parallel to Earth's axis. Then every hour is the same 15 degrees.
tricks.body_zh: 把晷針斜到當地的緯度（彰化 24 度），和地軸平行，每個鐘點就都是 15 度。

tricks.body_en: Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so the Sun and every shadow move 15 degrees an hour, about one and a half fists.
tricks.body_zh: 地球 24 小時轉 360 度，所以太陽和影子每小時移動 15 度，大約一個半拳頭。

tricks.title_en: Short in summer, long in winter
tricks.body_en: The noon shadow is shortest at the summer solstice and longest at the winter solstice. That is how the guibiao found the solstices.
tricks.body_zh: 正午的影子夏至最短、冬至最長；圭表就是這樣找出二至的。

tricks.title_en: Fast in November, slow in February
tricks.body_en: A Changhua sundial runs about 19 minutes ahead of the clock in early November and about 12 minutes behind in mid-February.
tricks.body_zh: 彰化的日晷十一月初比時鐘快大約 19 分鐘，二月中慢大約 12 分鐘。

activities.title_en: Find Solar Noon with a Stick
activities.title_zh: 用一根竿子找太陽正午

materials.en: A straight stick or pencil about 30 centimeters long, standing upright
materials.zh: 一根約 30 公分長的直竿或鉛筆，直立插好

materials.en: Chalk or small stones to mark the shadow
materials.zh: 粉筆或小石頭，用來標記影子

materials.en: A watch and the Today's Sundial table on this page
materials.zh: 一支手錶，以及本頁「今天彰化的日晷」表

steps.en: On a sunny day, start at 11:15 by the clock. Stand the stick straight up on flat ground.
steps.zh: 晴天裡，從時鐘 11:15 開始。在平地上把竿子直直立好。

steps.en: Every 5 minutes, mark the tip of the shadow and write the time beside it.
steps.zh: 每 5 分鐘標一次影子頂端的位置，並在旁邊寫上時間。

steps.en: Keep going until about 12:30. Find the mark with the shortest shadow.
steps.zh: 一直做到大約 12:30，找出影子最短的那一點。

steps.en: The time of the shortest shadow is solar noon. Compare it with the solar noon on this page.
steps.zh: 影子最短的時刻就是太陽正午。和本頁算出的太陽正午比一比。

steps.en: A line from the stick to the shortest mark points true north. Check it against a compass, and notice that they differ a little.
steps.zh: 從竿子到最短那一點的連線，就是真北。拿羅盤對照，會發現兩者有一點差距。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: in October and November, solar noon in Changhua comes well before 12:00, around 11:41 to 11:48, which surprises most students.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：十月、十一月時，彰化的太陽正午大約在 11:41 到 11:48 之間，比 12:00 早不少，學生通常很驚訝。

materials.en: A paper plate or card circle, with a pencil pushed through the center
materials.zh: 一個紙盤或圓形卡紙，中心插一枝鉛筆

materials.en: A protractor and a marker
materials.zh: 量角器和麥克筆

materials.en: A wedge of cardboard or clay to hold the dial at an angle
materials.zh: 一塊紙板或黏土，用來把晷面撐出角度

steps.en: Draw lines from the center every 15 degrees, like a clock face with 24 hours. Number the bottom line 12 and go around: 13, 14, 15... on one side and 11, 10, 9... on the other.
steps.zh: 從圓心每 15 度畫一條線，像 24 小時的鐘面。最下面那條標 12，一邊往 13、14、15……，另一邊往 11、10、9……。

steps.en: Push the pencil through the center so it sticks out on both sides. This is the gnomon.
steps.zh: 把鉛筆穿過圓心，兩面都露出來，這就是晷針。

steps.en: Outside, point the pencil toward true north and tilt it up 24 degrees, so the dial faces the sky at 66 degrees. Use the cardboard wedge to hold it steady.
steps.zh: 到戶外，讓鉛筆朝正北、往上斜 24 度，晷面就會以 66 度朝天。用紙板或黏土固定。

steps.en: Read the hour where the pencil's shadow falls. Then add or subtract the difference from the Today's Sundial table to get clock time.
steps.zh: 讀出鉛筆影子落在的鐘點，再依「今天彰化的日晷」表加減差距，換算成時鐘時間。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: between the March and September equinoxes the shadow falls on the top face; for the rest of the year, read the bottom face, just like the sundial in the 3D model.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：春分到秋分，影子落在晷面上面；其餘時間要看下面——和 3D 模型裡的日晷一樣。

lessons.title: How Big Is the Solar System?
lessons.blurb_en: Shrink the Sun to a basketball and Earth becomes a sesame seed 26 meters away. Fly out to Neptune on true distances, and race a flash of sunlight across the solar system.
lessons.blurb_zh: 把太陽縮成一顆籃球，地球就是 26 公尺外的一粒芝麻。照真實距離飛到海王星，再跟著一道陽光跑過整個太陽系。
lessons.big_idea_en: The planets are tiny compared with the distances between them, so the solar system is almost entirely empty space. No picture can show both the sizes and the distances to scale.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 和行星之間的距離比起來，行星本身小得驚人，所以太陽系幾乎全是空的。沒有一張圖能同時把大小和距離都照比例畫出來。

lab.title_zh: 真實的距離，可以調的大小
lab.how_en: The orbits and the planets' positions are real and to scale for today. Drag the size slider down to True size: the planets shrink until even Jupiter disappears, and only the colored dots show where they are. Then press Play to send a flash of light from the Sun and watch how long it takes to reach each planet. Zoom out step by step, from the inner planets to Neptune.
lab.how_zh: 軌道與行星今天的位置都是真實比例。把大小滑桿拉到「真實大小」：行星越縮越小，連木星都消失了，只剩彩色圓點標出位置。再按「播放」，從太陽發出一道光，看它多久才到每一顆行星。從內行星開始，一步步把鏡頭拉遠到海王星。

paras: Most pictures of the solar system show the planets lined up close together, like beads on a string. Those pictures are useful, but they cannot be true to scale. To see why, shrink the Sun to the size of a basketball. Earth becomes a sesame seed, about 26 meters away, and the Moon is a grain of sand less than seven centimeters from it. Mercury, Venus, and Mars are even smaller seeds, scattered within 40 meters of the ball.

Keep walking. Jupiter, the giant, is only a grape, 134 meters from the basketball. Saturn is a slightly smaller grape at 246 meters. Uranus and Neptune are peas, 495 and 776 meters out, almost two laps around a running track. On that scale, the nearest star after the Sun would be about 6,900 kilometers away, almost as far as Sydney is from Taiwan. Between all these tiny objects there is almost nothing at all. The solar system is mostly empty space.

How do we know such huge distances? Astronomers use a unit called the astronomical unit, or AU: the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometers. Measuring it took centuries. In 1672, astronomers in Paris and in French Guiana measured the position of Mars at the same time, and the small difference between their views gave the first good estimate. In 1769, Captain Cook sailed to Tahiti to time Venus crossing the face of the Sun for the same purpose. Today, radar and spacecraft measure these distances to within a few meters.

Even light needs time to cross the solar system. Light moves 300,000 kilometers every second, yet sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, so the Sun you see is the Sun of eight minutes ago. Sunlight reaches Jupiter in about 43 minutes and Neptune in about four hours. Radio messages to rovers on Mars take between 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the two planets are. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is now so far away that on November 18, 2026, its signals will take a full day to reach us.

People have always wondered how big the world is. The Chinese word for universe, yuzhou, joins two ideas: yu, all of space in every direction, and zhou, all of time from the past to the future. The astronomer Zhang Heng, almost 1,900 years ago, pictured the sky as an egg with Earth as the yolk inside. Telescopes later added two planets no one had seen before: Uranus in 1781 and Neptune in 1846. Neptune was first found with mathematics, from the way it tugged on Uranus, and only then spotted in the sky.

Beyond Neptune lie Pluto and many other icy worlds, and far beyond them, a vast cloud of comets that may reach a quarter of the way to the nearest star. The planets you found in Lesson 7 are tiny bright dots scattered across this enormous emptiness. Try the calculator below, build your own model at school, and walk the solar system for yourself.
paras_zh: 大部分太陽系的圖，都把行星畫得排排站、靠得很近，像一串珠子。這種圖很好用，但不可能照比例。想知道為什麼，就把太陽縮成一顆籃球：地球變成大約 26 公尺外的一粒芝麻，月亮是一粒細沙，離地球不到 7 公分。水星、金星、火星是更小的種子，散落在籃球 40 公尺以內。
繼續往前走。巨大的木星只是一顆葡萄，在籃球 134 公尺外；土星是稍小一點的葡萄，在 246 公尺外；天王星和海王星是豌豆，在 495 和 776 公尺外——差不多是跑道兩圈。照這個比例，太陽以外最近的恆星在大約 6,900 公里外，幾乎是台灣到雪梨的距離。在這些小東西之間，幾乎什麼都沒有。太陽系大部分是空的。
這麼大的距離，是怎麼知道的？天文學家用「天文單位」（AU）：地球到太陽的平均距離，大約 1.5 億公里。量出它花了好幾百年。1672 年，巴黎和法屬圭亞那的天文學家同時測量火星的位置，兩地看到的一點點差異，第一次給了可靠的估計。1769 年，庫克船長航向大溪地，為的也是在那裡計時金星從太陽前面經過。今天，雷達和太空船能把這些距離量到幾公尺以內。
連光穿過太陽系都需要時間。光每秒走 30 萬公里，陽光到地球仍要大約 8 分 20 秒，所以你看到的太陽，是 8 分鐘前的太陽。陽光到木星大約 43 分鐘，到海王星大約 4 小時。傳給火星探測車的無線電訊息要 3 到 22 分鐘，看兩顆行星當時的位置而定。1977 年發射的航海家一號現在非常遠，到 2026 年 11 月 18 日，它的訊號要整整一天才傳得回來。
人類一直在想世界有多大。中文的「宇宙」結合了兩個概念：「宇」是上下四方所有的空間，「宙」是從古到今所有的時間。將近 1,900 年前，天文學家張衡把天想像成一顆蛋，地球是裡面的蛋黃。望遠鏡後來又添了兩顆以前沒人見過的行星：1781 年的天王星和 1846 年的海王星。海王星是先用數學「算」出來的——從它拉扯天王星的方式推算位置——然後才在天上找到。
海王星以外還有冥王星和許多冰冷的小世界，更遠處是一大片彗星雲，可能延伸到往最近恆星四分之一的路程。你在第七課找到的行星，只是散落在這片廣大空曠中的小亮點。試試下面的計算器，在學校做一個自己的模型，親自走一趟太陽系。

cards.en: Space and Time in One Word
cards.quote_zh: 上下四方曰宇，往古來今曰宙。——《尸子》
cards.quote_en: "Up, down, and the four directions are yu; from ancient times to now is zhou." (The Shizi)
cards.body_en: More than 2,000 years ago, the Chinese word for universe already joined space and time, an idea that modern physics would return to.
cards.body_zh: 兩千多年前，中文的「宇宙」就把空間和時間放在一起，這個想法後來在現代物理裡又出現了。

cards.quote_zh: 渾天如雞子，天體圓如彈丸，地如雞中黃。——張衡〈渾天儀注〉
cards.quote_en: "The heavens are like a hen's egg, round as a crossbow pellet, and Earth is like the yolk." (Zhang Heng)
cards.body_en: Zhang Heng built a water-driven armillary sphere to show the turning sky around Earth. His egg was a model too: useful, even though the real sky has no shell.
cards.body_zh: 張衡造了水力推動的渾天儀，展示天繞著地轉。他的「雞蛋」也是一個模型：很好用，雖然真實的天空並沒有蛋殼。

cards.zh: 量出地球到太陽的距離
cards.body_en: In 1672, Giovanni Cassini in Paris and Jean Richer in French Guiana measured Mars at the same time and got about 140 million kilometers to the Sun. In 1769, observers around the world, including Captain Cook in Tahiti, timed Venus crossing the Sun to improve it.
cards.body_zh: 1672 年，巴黎的卡西尼和法屬圭亞那的里歇同時測量火星，算出太陽大約在 1.4 億公里外。1769 年，世界各地的觀測者（包括在大溪地的庫克船長）計時金星凌日，把數字量得更準。

cards.body_en: Uranus, found by William Herschel in 1781, was the first planet discovered with a telescope. Neptune was predicted in 1846 by Urbain Le Verrier from the way Uranus wobbled, and Johann Galle found it the same night he looked. Their Chinese names, the Sky King and the Sea King, follow the Greek and Roman gods.
cards.body_zh: 1781 年赫歇爾發現的天王星，是第一顆用望遠鏡找到的行星。海王星則是 1846 年勒維耶從天王星的「搖晃」算出來的，伽勒照著去看，當晚就找到了。中文名「天王」「海王」，來自希臘羅馬神話的天神與海神。

myths.myth_en: The planets are close together, like in textbook pictures.
myths.myth_zh: 行星彼此靠得很近，就像課本上的圖。
myths.fact_en: Those pictures shrink the distances so the planets fit. If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be 26 meters away and Neptune 776 meters away, and the planets would be seeds and peas.
myths.fact_zh: 那些圖把距離縮短了，行星才放得進來。如果太陽是一顆籃球，地球在 26 公尺外、海王星在 776 公尺外，而行星只是種子和豌豆。

myths.myth_en: The asteroid belt is packed with rocks, like in the movies.
myths.myth_zh: 小行星帶像電影裡一樣擠滿了石頭。
myths.fact_en: The asteroids are so spread out that spacecraft fly straight through the belt without needing to dodge. Standing on one asteroid, you could usually not see the next one with your eyes.
myths.fact_zh: 小行星分散得非常開，太空船直接穿過小行星帶，不需要閃躲。站在一顆小行星上，通常用肉眼看不到下一顆。

myths.myth_en: Sunlight reaches us instantly.
myths.myth_zh: 陽光一瞬間就照到我們。
myths.fact_en: It takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. If the Sun suddenly went dark, we would not know for eight minutes. Sunlight needs about four hours to reach Neptune.
myths.fact_zh: 要大約 8 分 20 秒。如果太陽突然熄滅，我們要過 8 分鐘才會知道。陽光到海王星要大約 4 小時。

myths.myth_en: Pluto is the ninth planet.
myths.myth_zh: 冥王星是第九顆行星。
myths.fact_en: Since 2006, astronomers have called Pluto a dwarf planet. It is smaller than our Moon and shares its part of space with many other icy worlds.
myths.fact_zh: 從 2006 年起，天文學家把冥王星歸為矮行星。它比我們的月亮還小，和許多冰冷的小天體共用那一帶的空間。

tricks.body_zh: 陽光到地球大約 8 分 20 秒；1 天文單位大約等於 8 光分。

materials.en: A basketball for the Sun

materials.en: Seeds and small fruits: sesame seeds, a grape, and two peas

materials.en: The calculator on this page and a long open space, such as a school track or a quiet road

steps.en: Put the basketball at the start. Use the calculator to find each planet's distance.
steps.zh: 把籃球放在起點，用計算器查出每顆行星的距離。

steps.en: Walk out together and set down each planet as you reach it: sesame seeds for Mercury to Mars within 40 meters, a grape for Jupiter at 134 meters.
steps.zh: 大家一起往外走，到了就放下行星：40 公尺內放水星到火星的芝麻，134 公尺放木星的葡萄。

steps.en: If you have room, keep going: Saturn at 246 meters, Uranus at 495, and Neptune at 776, almost two laps of a 400-meter track.

steps.en: Look back at the basketball from Neptune. Then discuss: where would the nearest star be? (About 6,900 kilometers away.)
steps.zh: 從海王星回頭看籃球。再討論：最近的恆星會在哪裡？（大約 6,900 公里外。）

activities.tip_en: Safety tip: walk the route ahead of time, keep everyone together, and stay off busy roads. A walk around the school track works well.

lessons.title: How Far Away Are the Stars?
lessons.blurb_en: Hold up your thumb and blink: it jumps. Earth plays the same trick with its orbit to measure the stars. Then find out when tonight's starlight set out, from the year you were born back to the Ming dynasty.
lessons.blurb_zh: 伸出拇指、輪流閉一隻眼，拇指會跳動。地球用繞太陽的軌道玩同一招，量出星星的距離。再看看今晚的星光是哪一年出發的：從你出生那年，一路到明朝。
lessons.big_idea_en: Stars are so far away that we measure them in light-years. As Earth goes around the Sun, a nearby star shifts back and forth a tiny bit against the faraway stars behind it. This shift is called parallax, and the farther away the star, the smaller the shift.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 星星遠到要用「光年」來量。地球繞著太陽走，近的星星會在更遠的星空前面微微來回移動，這叫做「視差」；星星越遠，移動得越少。

lab.title_en: Two Eyes Half a Year Apart
lab.how_en: Earth today (blue) and Earth half a year later (orange) look at the same nearby star. Their sight lines land on the faraway stars at two different spots: that shift is parallax. Pick a star and watch the two lines squeeze together as the star gets farther away. On the right, a telescope view shows the tiny loop each star traces in a year, all at the same zoom. Then switch to 20, 100, and 2,000 light-years to see where the Sun's real neighbors are.
lab.how_zh: 今天的地球（藍）和半年後的地球（橘）看著同一顆近星，兩條視線落在遠方星空的兩個不同位置：這段差距就是視差。換一顆星，看星越遠、兩條線就夾得越緊。右邊是望遠鏡裡看到的：每顆星一年畫出的小圈圈，放大倍率都一樣。再切換到 20、100、2,000 光年，看看太陽真正的鄰居在哪裡。

legend.en: Blue and orange lines: sight lines from Earth today and from Earth half a year later

paras: Look up on a clear night, and all the stars seem to sit on the same dark dome, as if they were the same distance away. They are not. Some stars are close neighbors of the Sun, and others are hundreds of times farther. The distances are so huge that kilometers are no help, so astronomers use the light-year: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers. A light-year is a distance, not a time. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light-years away.

How can you measure the distance to something you can never visit? Try this. Hold up your thumb at arm's length and look at it with one eye. Then blink and look with the other eye. Your thumb seems to jump against the background. This jump is called parallax. Bring your thumb closer to your face, and it jumps more; move it farther away, and it jumps less. Your brain uses the small difference between your two eyes to judge how far away things are.

Astronomers use the same trick, but with two eyes much farther apart. Every six months, Earth reaches the opposite side of its orbit, about 300 million kilometers from where it was. Seen from these two places, a nearby star shifts a tiny bit against much more distant stars in the background. Measure the angle of that shift, draw a triangle, and you can work out the distance. The angle is tiny: even for Proxima Centauri, it is like the width of a coin seen from more than five kilometers away. Farther stars shift even less.

For more than 2,000 years, people looked for this shift and could not find it. Some ancient Greek thinkers even took this as proof that Earth does not move. The shift was simply too small for their eyes. At last, in 1838, the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of a faint star called 61 Cygni and found it was about 10 light-years away. Today we know it is 11.4. In 1989, the European satellite Hipparcos began making precise measurements from above the blurry air, for about 118,000 stars, and its successor, Gaia, has measured nearly 1.5 billion.

Because light needs time to travel, looking at the stars means looking into the past. The light from Sirius that reaches you tonight left it about eight and a half years ago. Vega's light left 25 years ago, and Betelgeuse's light began its journey around 500 years ago, during China's Ming dynasty. The poet Li Bai wrote that people today cannot see the Moon of ancient times, yet this same Moon once shone on the ancients. Starlight turns his idea around: tonight you can see light that set out while people of the past were alive.

Parallax is the first step on a ladder of distances. It works well for nearby stars, but for very distant ones the shift is too small to measure well, so astronomers use other clues, such as how bright a star really is. Even some famous bright stars, like Deneb, still have uncertain distances. Use the list below to find out when tonight's starlight left home, and look for your own birthday star: a star whose light set out in the year you were born.
paras_zh: 晴朗的夜晚抬頭看，所有的星星好像都貼在同一個黑色的圓頂上，跟我們一樣遠。其實不是。有些星是太陽的近鄰，有些卻遠了好幾百倍。這些距離大到用公里來量已經沒有意義，所以天文學家用「光年」：光走一年的距離，大約 9.46 兆公里。光年是距離，不是時間。除了太陽以外最近的恆星是比鄰星，大約在 4.2 光年外。
一個永遠去不了的地方，要怎麼量它有多遠？試試看：把拇指伸直到手臂那麼遠，先用一隻眼睛看，再眨眼換另一隻眼睛看。拇指好像在背景前面跳了一下。這一跳就叫做「視差」。把拇指移近臉，它跳得更多；移遠一點，它就跳得少。你的大腦就是用兩隻眼睛之間的這一點點差異，來判斷東西有多遠。
天文學家用的是同一招，只是兩隻「眼睛」離得遠多了。每隔半年，地球就走到軌道的另一邊，離原來的位置大約 3 億公里。從這兩個地方看，一顆近的星會在背景中遠得多的星星前面，移動一點點。量出這個位移的角度，畫一個三角形，就能算出距離。這個角度非常小：就算是比鄰星，也只像從 5 公里外看一枚硬幣的寬度。更遠的星，移動得更少。

兩千多年來，人們一直在找這個位移，卻找不到。有些古希臘的思想家甚至把它當成「地球不會動」的證據。其實只是位移太小，肉眼看不出來。直到 1838 年，德國天文學家貝索量到一顆暗星「天鵝座 61」的視差，算出它大約在 10 光年外；今天我們知道是 11.4 光年。1989 年，歐洲的依巴谷衛星（Hipparcos）開始在模糊的大氣層之上做精確測量，量了大約 11.8 萬顆星；它的接班人蓋亞（Gaia）已經量了將近 15 億顆。
光走路需要時間，所以看星星就是在看過去。今晚到達你眼睛的天狼星光，大約是 8 年半前出發的；織女星的光是 25 年前出發的；參宿四的光大約 500 年前、中國的明朝時就踏上了旅程。李白寫過「今人不見古時月，今月曾經照古人」。星光正好倒過來：今晚你看到的光，出發時，古時候的人還活著。
視差是量距離這座「梯子」的第一階。它很適合量近的星，但星太遠時位移小到量不準，天文學家就改用別的線索，例如星星本身到底有多亮。就連天津四這樣有名的亮星，距離到今天還說不準。用下面的清單查查今晚的星光是哪一年出發的，也找一找你自己的生日星：它的光，就在你出生那年出發。

The German astronomer Friedrich Bessel, in 1838. He measured the parallax of the star 61 Cygni.

neighbors.note_en: The nearest star after the Sun: a small red dwarf, too faint to see without a telescope and too far south to see from Taiwan.
neighbors.note_zh: 除了太陽以外最近的恆星：一顆小小的紅矮星，肉眼看不到，在台灣也因為太偏南而看不見。

neighbors.note_en: Two Sun-like stars that circle each other. Together they shine as the third-brightest star at night, but from Taiwan they barely clear the southern horizon.
neighbors.note_zh: 兩顆和太陽很像的星互相繞轉，合起來是夜空第三亮的星；在台灣只會貼著南方地平線露個臉。

neighbors.note_en: The brightest star in the night sky, partly because it is so close.
neighbors.note_zh: 夜空中最亮的恆星，原因之一就是它離我們很近。

neighbors.note_en: Bessel's star, the first to have its distance measured, in 1838. It drifts quickly across the sky, a clue that it is close.
neighbors.note_zh: 貝索的星：1838 年第一顆量到距離的恆星。它在天上移動得很快，暗示它離我們很近。

neighbors.note_en: The Cowherd of the Qixi story, about 15 light-years from the Weaver Girl.
neighbors.note_zh: 七夕故事裡的牛郎，和織女相隔大約 15 光年。

neighbors.note_en: The Weaver Girl, high overhead on summer evenings.
neighbors.note_zh: 七夕故事裡的織女，夏天晚上高掛頭頂。

neighbors.note_en: A red supergiant in Orion. Its parallax is so small that its distance is still debated.
neighbors.note_zh: 獵戶座的紅超巨星。視差太小，距離到現在還有爭論。

neighbors.note_en: One of the most powerful stars we can see. Hipparcos could barely measure its shift, and other methods suggest it may be even farther.
neighbors.note_zh: 肉眼看得到的恆星裡最強大的之一。依巴谷衛星幾乎量不出它的位移，其他方法甚至認為它更遠。

lessons.neighbors_note_en: Distances come from each star's parallax, measured by the Hipparcos satellite. The farther the star, the wider the range of possible distances. "Light left" is worked out for today's date.
lessons.neighbors_note_zh: 距離由依巴谷衛星量到的視差算出：星越遠，可能的距離範圍越寬。「光出發於」照今天的日期現算。

tonight.lead_en: Every bright star above Changhua at 9 p.m. tonight, nearest first, with the year its light set out. The list is calculated in your browser for today's date.
tonight.lead_zh: 今晚九點彰化天上的每一顆亮星，由近到遠排列，附上它的光是哪一年出發的。清單在瀏覽器裡照今天的日期現算。

birthday.lead_en: Type the year you were born. These stars are about as many light-years away as you are years old, so the light reaching you tonight left them around the time you were born.
birthday.lead_zh: 輸入你出生的年份。這幾顆星離我們的光年數，差不多就是你的歲數：今晚到達的光，大約在你出生那年出發。

culture_cards.title_en: Distance and Time in the Sky
culture_cards.lead_en: Poets, stargazers, and astronomers East and West have all wondered how far away the sky is.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 東西方的詩人、觀星者和天文學家，都想過天到底有多遠。

cards.zh: 牛郎織女相隔 15 光年
cards.quote_zh: 盈盈一水間，脈脈不得語。——〈迢迢牽牛星〉（古詩十九首）
cards.quote_en: "Just one clear stream between them, they gaze and cannot speak." (Nineteen Old Poems)
cards.body_en: In the story, the Cowherd (Altair) and the Weaver Girl (Vega) meet once a year on a bridge of magpies. In space they are about 15 light-years apart, so even a message sent at the speed of light would take 15 years to arrive.
cards.body_zh: 故事裡，牛郎（牛郎星）和織女（織女星）每年在鵲橋相會一次。在太空中，兩顆星相隔大約 15 光年：就算用光速傳訊息，也要 15 年才收得到。

cards.quote_zh: 今人不見古時月，今月曾經照古人。——李白〈把酒問月〉
cards.quote_en: "People today do not see the Moon of old times, yet today's Moon once shone on the people of old." (Li Bai)
cards.body_en: Starlight turns the poem around. The light you see tonight from Betelgeuse set out about 500 years ago, during the Ming dynasty. The farther the star, the older its light.
cards.body_zh: 星光把這首詩倒過來：今晚看到的參宿四星光，大約 500 年前、明朝時就出發了。星越遠，光越古老。

cards.body_en: Friedrich Bessel watched 61 Cygni for more than a year and found a parallax of about 0.3 arcseconds, smaller than the width of a hair seen from 30 meters away. It was the shift people had looked for since ancient Greece, and the first distance ever measured to a star.
cards.body_zh: 貝索觀測天鵝座 61 一年多，量到大約 0.3 角秒的視差，比從 30 公尺外看一根頭髮還細。這是從古希臘就有人在找的位移，也是人類第一次量出到恆星的距離。

cards.body_en: The ancient Chinese book Zhoubi Suanjing compared the shadows of poles in different places and worked out that the Sun was 80,000 li high. Using two viewpoints and a triangle was the right idea. The answer was wrong only because the book assumed Earth was flat.
cards.body_zh: 古代的《周髀算經》比較不同地方的竿影，推算出「日高八萬里」。用兩個觀測點加上三角形，方法是對的；答案錯，只是因為書裡假設大地是平的。

myths.myth_en: A light-year is a measure of time.
myths.myth_zh: 光年是時間單位。
myths.fact_en: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers. It uses time to describe length, just like saying a store is "ten minutes away."
myths.fact_zh: 光年是距離：光走一年的路程，大約 9.46 兆公里。它是用時間來描述長度，就像說「商店在十分鐘路程外」。

myths.myth_en: All the stars are the same distance away, stuck on a dome.
myths.myth_zh: 所有星星都一樣遠，貼在同一個圓頂上。
myths.fact_en: They only look that way because they are too far away for our eyes to judge depth. In Orion alone, Bellatrix is about 250 light-years away, Betelgeuse about 500, and Rigel about 860.
myths.fact_zh: 看起來是這樣，只是因為它們太遠，眼睛分不出遠近。光是獵戶座：參宿五大約 250 光年，參宿四約 500 光年，參宿七約 860 光年。

myths.myth_en: The brightest stars are the closest ones.
myths.myth_zh: 越亮的星，離我們越近。
myths.fact_en: Within 20 light-years, Hipparcos measured 74 stars, and only 17 of them can be seen without a telescope. Most of the Sun's neighbors, including Proxima Centauri, are dim red dwarfs. Deneb shines brightly even though it is more than 1,000 light-years away, because it gives off tens of thousands of times more light than the Sun.
myths.fact_zh: 20 光年內，依巴谷衛星量到 74 顆星，肉眼看得到的只有 17 顆。太陽的鄰居大多是暗淡的紅矮星，比鄰星也是。天津四在 1,000 多光年外仍然很亮，因為它發出的光是太陽的好幾萬倍。

myths.myth_en: Many of the stars we see have already burned out.
myths.myth_zh: 我們看到的星星，很多早就熄滅了。
myths.fact_en: Starlight is old, but not that old. Almost every star you can see without a telescope is within a few thousand light-years, and stars shine for millions or billions of years. Their light left them only recently, as stars go, so nearly all of them are still shining.
myths.fact_zh: 星光很古老，但沒那麼古老。肉眼看得到的星，幾乎都在幾千光年以內，而恆星能發光幾百萬到幾十億年。以恆星的一生來說，它們的光才剛出發不久，所以幾乎都還亮著。

tricks.body_en: Blink one eye, then the other: near things jump more than far things. That jump is parallax.
tricks.body_zh: 輪流閉一隻眼：近的東西跳得多，遠的跳得少。這一跳就是視差。

tricks.body_en: Not a time. One light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometers, or 63,000 times the distance from Earth to the Sun.
tricks.body_zh: 不是時間。1 光年約 9.5 兆公里，是地球到太陽距離的 6.3 萬倍。

tricks.body_en: Proxima Centauri, Sirius, and Vega are about 4.2, 8.6, and 25 light-years away.
tricks.body_zh: 比鄰星、天狼星、織女星大約在 4.2、8.6、25 光年外。

tricks.title_zh: 看得越遠，看到越久以前
tricks.body_en: Light from a star 500 light-years away left it about 500 years ago.
tricks.body_zh: 500 光年外的星，它的光大約是 500 年前出發的。

materials.en: A pencil and a tape measure
materials.zh: 一枝鉛筆、一條捲尺

materials.en: Ten sticky notes numbered 1 to 10, stuck in a row on a wall about 10 cm apart
materials.zh: 十張寫上 1 到 10 的便利貼，在牆上排成一列，每張相隔約 10 公分

materials.en: A worksheet with three columns: pencil distance, number of notes it jumps, and notes
materials.zh: 一張學習單，分三欄：鉛筆距離、跳過幾張便利貼、備註

steps.en: Stand 3 meters from the wall. Hold the pencil upright at arm's length, in front of the sticky notes.
steps.zh: 站在離牆 3 公尺的地方，把鉛筆直立、手臂伸直，擋在便利貼前面。

steps.en: Close your left eye and note which number the pencil covers. Switch eyes and count how many notes it jumps.
steps.zh: 閉上左眼，記下鉛筆擋住哪個號碼；換眼睛看，數數它跳過幾張。

steps.en: Repeat with the pencil at half an arm's length, then as close as you can still see it clearly. Record each jump.
steps.zh: 把鉛筆移到半個手臂遠，再移到最近還看得清楚的地方，各做一次，記下跳了幾張。

steps.en: Discuss: when the pencil is twice as close, what happens to the jump? (It roughly doubles.) Astronomers use the same rule to turn a shift into a distance.
steps.zh: 討論：鉛筆近了一倍，跳的距離怎麼變？（大約變兩倍。）天文學家就是用這個規律，把位移換算成距離。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: your eyes are about 6 cm apart, while Earth's "eyes" are 300 million kilometers apart. Then open the 3D model and compare the shift of Proxima Centauri with Betelgeuse.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：我們的兩眼相距約 6 公分，地球的兩隻「眼睛」相距 3 億公里。接著打開 3D 模型，比較比鄰星和參宿四的位移。

materials.en: The birthday-star finder on this page
materials.zh: 本頁的生日星查詢

materials.en: The sky map in Lesson 5 (tonight's sky over Changhua) or a printed star map
materials.zh: 第五課的星空圖（今晚彰化的星空），或一張印出來的星圖

materials.en: Paper and colored pencils for a class timeline
materials.zh: 做全班時間軸用的紙和彩色鉛筆

steps.en: Type your birth year into the finder. Write down your star's name, its distance, and the best month to see it.
steps.zh: 在查詢框輸入出生年份，記下你的星的名字、距離，以及最適合看它的月份。

steps.en: Find the star on the Lesson 5 sky map or a star map, and mark it.
steps.zh: 在第五課的星空圖或星圖上找到這顆星，做個記號。

steps.en: Make a class timeline: put each student's star on it, along with the year its light set out.
steps.zh: 做一條全班的時間軸：把每個人的星，連同光出發的年份，貼上去。

steps.en: Discuss: why will you need a different star next year? (Next year you will be a year older, so you need a star one light-year farther away.)
steps.zh: 討論：為什麼明年要換一顆星？（明年你大一歲，要找再遠一光年的星。）

activities.tip_en: Tip: distances have small errors, so any star within about half a light-year of your age counts. Parents and grandparents can find theirs too; the finder goes out to 100 light-years.
activities.tip_zh: 提示：距離有小小的誤差，跟你歲數相差半光年以內都算數。爸媽和爺爺奶奶也能找自己的生日星：查詢範圍到 100 光年。

lessons.title: Where Do Meteor Showers Come From?
lessons.blurb_en: A shooting star is a grain of comet dust burning up 100 kilometers overhead. Ride with Earth as it plows through a comet's trail on the same dates every year, and plan your night for the next shower over Changhua.
lessons.blurb_zh: 流星是一粒彗星碎屑，在 100 公里高空燒掉的光。跟著地球每年在同一天穿過彗星留下的碎屑帶，再規劃你看下一場流星雨的夜晚。
lessons.big_idea_en: Comets leave trails of dust along their orbits. Every year, Earth passes through the same trails on about the same dates, and the dust burns up in our air as a meteor shower.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 彗星沿著軌道留下一條條碎屑帶。地球每年在差不多同一天穿過同一條碎屑帶，碎屑撞進大氣燒掉，就成了流星雨。

lab.title_en: Earth Plows Through a Comet's Dust
lab.title_zh: 地球穿過彗星的碎屑帶
lab.how_en: Pick a shower. The colored loop is the orbit of its parent comet, and the glowing dots are the dust left along the way. Press Play: Earth travels around the Sun on real dates, and on about the same dates every year it reaches the gold ring and passes through the dust. Switch to Near Earth to watch the grains hit our air. On the right is the night of the peak over Changhua: every meteor seems to fly out of one point, the radiant.
lab.how_zh: 選一個流星雨。彩色的圈是母彗星的軌道，發光的小點是它一路留下的碎屑。按「播放」：地球照真實日期繞太陽，每年差不多同一天走到金色圓圈，穿過碎屑帶。切換到「靠近地球」，看碎屑撞進大氣。右邊是極大那一夜的彰化天空：每顆流星都像從同一點射出來，那一點叫做輻射點。

legend.en: Colored dots: dust left along the parent's orbit (the trail is drawn wider than it really is)
legend.zh: 彩色小點：沿著母天體軌道留下的碎屑（碎屑帶畫得比實際寬）

legend.en: Gold ring: where Earth is every year at the shower's peak
legend.zh: 金色圓圈：每年流星雨極大時，地球所在的位置

legend.en: Yellow lines near Earth: grains arriving from the direction of the radiant
legend.zh: 地球旁的黃色短線：從輻射點方向迎面而來的碎屑

legend.en: Orbits and dates are real; the Sun and Earth are drawn much larger
legend.zh: 軌道與日期是真的；太陽和地球畫得大很多

lab.scale_en: Orbits are to scale (1 AU = 10 units), and Earth moves on real dates. The Sun and Earth are enlarged, the dust trail is drawn wider than it is, and the far ends of long comet orbits are cut off at 6 AU. The sky chart shows the real radiant, stars, and Moon for the peak night.
lab.scale_zh: 軌道照比例（1 天文單位＝10 單位），地球照真實日期移動。太陽和地球放大了，碎屑帶也畫得比實際寬；長週期彗星的軌道外段在 6 天文單位處截掉。右邊的星圖用的是極大夜真實的輻射點、星星與月亮。

paras: On a dark night, you may see a quick streak of light shoot across the sky. People call it a shooting star, but it is not a star at all. It is a meteor: a speck of space dust, often smaller than a grain of sand, slamming into Earth's air at up to 70 kilometers per second. The air in front of it gets so hot that it glows, about 100 kilometers above the ground, and the tiny grain burns up in less than a second.

Where does all that dust come from? Most of it comes from comets. A comet is a chunk of ice and rock a few kilometers across that travels around the Sun on a long, stretched orbit. When it comes close to the Sun, some of the ice turns to gas and blows dust out into space. Over hundreds and thousands of years, the dust spreads out along the comet's orbit like a trail of crumbs.

Earth's orbit crosses some of these trails. Every year, when Earth reaches the same point in its orbit, it plows through the same trail of dust, and we see a meteor shower. That is why each shower returns on about the same dates every year: the Perseids in August, the Orionids in October, and the Geminids in December. Halley's Comet gives us two showers, because Earth passes close to its orbit twice a year, in May and in October.

During a shower, trace the meteors backward, and they all seem to come from one spot in the sky, called the radiant. The grains are really moving side by side along parallel paths, but perspective makes them look as if they spread out from a single point, just as railroad tracks seem to meet in the distance. Each shower is named after the constellation where its radiant lies: the Perseids come from Perseus, and the Leonids from Leo. More meteors fall after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward along its orbit, like the windshield of a car driving through rain.

People have watched meteor showers for thousands of years. In 687 BCE, the Chinese chronicle known as the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded that in the middle of the night, "stars fell like rain," one of the oldest records of a meteor shower anywhere. In November 1833, the Leonids filled the sky over North America with tens of thousands of meteors an hour. The American scientist Denison Olmsted noticed that they all came from one point in Leo and concluded that they must come from space. In 1866, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli showed that the Perseids follow the same path as a comet, Swift–Tuttle.

You do not need a telescope to watch a meteor shower. Your eyes are the best tool, because they can take in the whole sky at once. Find a dark place away from city lights, lie back, and give your eyes about 20 minutes to get used to the dark. Be patient: meteors often come in bursts, with quiet minutes in between. A bright Moon washes out the fainter meteors, so check the list below to see when the next showers peak over Changhua and how bright the Moon will be.
paras_zh: 黑暗的夜裡，你可能會看到一道光一閃劃過天空。大家叫它「流星」，英文說 shooting star（會飛的星），但它根本不是星星，而是一粒太空塵埃，常常比一粒沙還小，以每秒最快 70 公里的速度撞進地球的大氣。它前方的空氣被壓得非常熱而發光，高度大約在地面上 100 公里，這粒小小的碎屑不到一秒就燒光了。
這麼多塵埃是從哪裡來的？大部分來自彗星。彗星是一團幾公里大的冰和岩石，沿著又長又扁的軌道繞太陽。它靠近太陽時，有些冰變成氣體，把塵埃吹到太空中。經過幾百、幾千年，這些塵埃沿著彗星的軌道散開，像一路撒下的麵包屑。
地球的軌道和其中一些碎屑帶交錯。每年地球走到軌道上同一個位置時，就穿過同一條碎屑帶，我們便看到流星雨。所以每個流星雨每年都在差不多同一天回來：英仙座流星雨在八月，獵戶座流星雨在十月，雙子座流星雨在十二月。哈雷彗星送給我們兩場流星雨，因為地球每年兩次經過它的軌道附近：五月一次，十月一次。
流星雨的時候，把流星往回延長，它們好像都從天上同一點射出來，這一點叫做「輻射點」。其實碎屑是並排沿著平行的路線飛行，只是透視讓它們看起來從一點散開，就像鐵軌在遠方好像交會在一起。每個流星雨都以輻射點所在的星座命名：英仙座流星雨從英仙座來，獅子座流星雨從獅子座來。午夜以後流星比較多，因為那時你所在的這一面地球朝著軌道前進的方向，就像在雨中開車時的擋風玻璃。
人類觀看流星雨已經好幾千年了。西元前 687 年，中國的《春秋》記載：「夜中，星隕如雨」，是世界上最古老的流星雨紀錄之一。1833 年 11 月，獅子座流星雨在北美洲的天空下，一小時有好幾萬顆流星。美國科學家奧姆斯特德注意到它們都從獅子座的同一點射出來，於是推論它們一定來自太空。1866 年，義大利天文學家斯基亞帕雷利證明，英仙座流星雨和一顆彗星「斯威夫特－塔特爾」走的是同一條路線。
看流星雨不需要望遠鏡。眼睛就是最好的工具，因為它能一次看到整片天空。找一個遠離城市燈光的暗處，躺下來，給眼睛大約 20 分鐘適應黑暗。要有耐心：流星常常一陣一陣地來，中間會安靜好幾分鐘。明亮的月光會蓋掉比較暗的流星，所以看看下面的清單，查查接下來的流星雨什麼時候在彰化達到極大，那時月亮有多亮。
questions: What is a meteor?
Why does each meteor shower come back on about the same dates every year?
Why do the meteors in a shower seem to come from one point in the sky?
answers: A tiny piece of space dust, often smaller than a grain of sand, that burns up in Earth's air about 100 kilometers above the ground.
Earth reaches the same point in its orbit on the same dates each year, so it passes through the same trail of comet dust.
The dust grains travel along parallel paths, and perspective makes parallel lines look as if they spread out from a single point, the radiant.

showers.note_en: A short, sharp peak in early January, named after an old constellation that is no longer used. Its parent may be a worn-out comet.
showers.note_zh: 一月初短而集中的極大，名字來自一個已經不用的古星座。母天體可能是一顆耗盡的彗星。

showers.note_en: Possibly the shower in the oldest record, from 687 BCE. Its comet comes back only once every 415 years.
showers.note_zh: 可能就是西元前 687 年那筆最古老紀錄裡的流星雨。它的彗星每 415 年才回來一次。

showers.note_en: Dust from Halley's Comet. Watch before dawn in early May; the radiant rises only a few hours before the Sun.
showers.note_zh: 哈雷彗星的碎屑。五月初黎明前看；輻射點在日出前幾小時才升起。

showers.note_en: The favorite summer shower. Its comet is about 26 kilometers across, the largest object that passes near Earth again and again.
showers.note_zh: 最受歡迎的夏季流星雨。它的彗星大約 26 公里寬，是一再接近地球的天體裡最大的。

showers.note_en: More dust from Halley's Comet, hitting us almost head-on. Fast meteors like these often leave glowing trails.
showers.note_zh: 又是哈雷彗星的碎屑，幾乎迎面撞來。這麼快的流星常會留下發光的餘跡。

showers.note_en: The fastest shower. Usually modest, but around the times its comet returns, about every 33 years, it has stormed, as in 1833, 1966, and 2001.
showers.note_zh: 最快的流星雨。平常不多，但在它的彗星回歸前後（約每 33 年）曾經爆發成「流星暴」，例如 1833、1966、2001 年。

showers.note_en: Usually the richest shower of the year, and good for children: the radiant rises in the evening. Its parent is a rocky asteroid, not an icy comet.
showers.note_zh: 通常是一年中最豐富的流星雨，也適合小朋友：輻射點傍晚就升起。母天體是岩石小行星，不是冰質彗星。

showers.note_en: A quiet shower just before Christmas. From Taiwan, the radiant near the Little Dipper never sets.
showers.note_zh: 聖誕節前一個安靜的流星雨。在台灣，小北斗旁的輻射點整夜不會落下。

lessons.showers_note_en: ZHR is the number of meteors one observer would see in an hour under a perfect dark sky with the radiant overhead; real counts are lower. Speed is how fast the grains hit our air.
lessons.showers_note_zh: ZHR（天頂每時出現率）是理想暗空、輻射點在頭頂時，一個人一小時能看到的流星數；實際看到的會比較少。速度是碎屑撞進大氣的速度。

culture_cards.lead_en: From ancient chronicles to modern science, meteor showers have puzzled and amazed people for thousands of years.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 從古代史書到現代科學，流星雨讓人困惑、驚嘆了好幾千年。

cards.quote_zh: 夏四月辛卯，夜，恆星不見。夜中，星隕如雨。——《春秋》莊公七年
cards.quote_en: "In summer, in the fourth month, at night the usual stars could not be seen. In the middle of the night, stars fell like rain." (Spring and Autumn Annals)
cards.body_en: This line is one of the oldest meteor shower records in the world. The date fits the Lyrids, which still return every April.
cards.body_zh: 這一句是世界上最古老的流星雨紀錄之一。日期和每年四月回來的天琴座流星雨吻合。

cards.body_en: The Chinese character for comet means "broom," for its sweeping tail, and people called comets broom stars. Chinese astronomers recorded Halley's Comet on nearly every return since 240 BCE, long before anyone knew it was the same comet.
cards.body_zh: 「彗」字的本義是掃帚，因為彗星的尾巴像在掃地，民間叫它掃帚星。從西元前 240 年起，中國天文官幾乎記錄了哈雷彗星的每一次回歸，那時還沒有人知道這些是同一顆彗星。

cards.body_en: The Leonid storm of November 1833 frightened and amazed people across North America. Denison Olmsted collected reports and saw that every meteor came from one point in Leo, which moved with the stars. The meteors had to come from space, not from the air.
cards.body_zh: 1833 年 11 月的獅子座流星暴，讓整個北美洲的人又害怕又驚奇。奧姆斯特德收集各地的目擊紀錄，發現每顆流星都從獅子座的同一點射出，而且那一點跟著星星一起移動——所以流星一定來自太空，而不是空氣裡。

cards.body_en: Giovanni Schiaparelli worked out the orbit of the Perseid grains and found it matched the comet Swift–Tuttle, seen in 1862. It was the first proof that meteor showers are made of comet dust.
cards.body_zh: 斯基亞帕雷利算出英仙座流星的軌道，發現它和 1862 年出現的斯威夫特－塔特爾彗星一模一樣。這是「流星雨是彗星碎屑」的第一個證據。

myths.myth_en: Shooting stars are stars falling from the sky.
myths.myth_zh: 流星是天上掉下來的星星。
myths.fact_en: A meteor is a grain of dust burning up about 100 kilometers overhead. Real stars are suns, light-years away, and they do not fall.
myths.fact_zh: 流星是一粒塵埃，在頭頂大約 100 公里高的地方燒掉。真正的恆星是遠在好幾光年外的太陽，不會掉下來。

myths.myth_en: The meteors come from the constellation they are named after.
myths.myth_zh: 流星是從命名的那個星座來的。
myths.fact_en: The radiant is only the direction the grains come from, seen in perspective. The dust is inside our solar system, while the stars of Perseus are hundreds of light-years away.
myths.fact_zh: 輻射點只是碎屑飛來的方向，加上透視效果。碎屑就在太陽系裡，而英仙座的星星遠在幾百光年外。

myths.myth_en: You need a telescope to see a meteor shower.
myths.myth_zh: 看流星雨要用望遠鏡。
myths.fact_en: A telescope shows only a tiny patch of sky, and meteors can appear anywhere. Your eyes, which see the whole sky, are the best tool.
myths.fact_zh: 望遠鏡只看得到一小塊天空，流星卻可能出現在任何地方。能看見整片天空的眼睛才是最好的工具。

myths.myth_en: Meteors from a shower often reach the ground.
myths.myth_zh: 流星雨的流星常常會掉到地面上。
myths.fact_en: Shower grains are tiny, fragile bits of comet dust, and they burn up completely. The rare rocks that land, called meteorites, come from bigger chunks, mostly pieces of asteroids.
myths.fact_zh: 流星雨的碎屑是又小又脆的彗星塵埃，會完全燒光。少數落到地面的石頭叫隕石，來自比較大的岩塊，大多是小行星的碎片。

tricks.body_en: A meteor shower is Earth plowing through the crumbs a comet left behind.
tricks.body_zh: 流星雨，就是地球穿過彗星留下的碎屑帶。

tricks.body_en: Earth crosses each trail at the same point in its orbit, so each shower comes back on about the same dates every year.
tricks.body_zh: 地球每年在軌道同一點穿過同一條碎屑帶，所以流星雨年年差不多同一天回來。

tricks.body_en: If a meteor's path points back to the radiant, it belongs to the shower.
tricks.body_zh: 把流星的路徑往回延長，如果指向輻射點，它就屬於這場流星雨。

tricks.body_en: After midnight, your side of Earth faces forward, like a windshield in the rain.
tricks.body_zh: 午夜以後，你這一面的地球朝前方，就像雨中的擋風玻璃。

materials.en: A ball of yarn and some tape
materials.zh: 一捲毛線和膠帶

materials.en: A long hallway or a playground
materials.zh: 一條長走廊或一片操場

materials.en: Five or six students to hold the yarn
materials.zh: 五、六位同學幫忙拉線

steps.en: Stretch four or five pieces of yarn, each about 10 meters long, side by side and parallel, about 30 cm apart, at about head height.
steps.zh: 拉出四、五條約 10 公尺長的毛線，彼此平行、相隔約 30 公分，高度大約在頭部。

steps.en: One student stands at one end, just under the yarn, and looks along it toward the far end.
steps.zh: 請一位同學站在一端、線的正下方，沿著毛線往遠方看。

steps.en: Ask: do the lines look parallel? (No: they seem to spread out from a point at the far end.)
steps.zh: 問問看：這些線看起來平行嗎？（不平行：它們好像從遠方一點散開。）

steps.en: Explain: the meteors in a shower also travel side by side. The point they seem to come from is the radiant.
steps.zh: 說明：流星雨的碎屑也是並排飛行的；它們好像射出來的那一點，就是輻射點。

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: then open the sky chart next to the 3D model and watch the meteors spread out from the radiant.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：接著打開 3D 模型旁的星圖，看流星從輻射點散開。

materials.en: The list of upcoming showers on this page
materials.zh: 本頁「接下來的流星雨」清單

materials.en: A mat or reclining chair, warm clothes, and a red flashlight
materials.zh: 一張墊子或躺椅、保暖衣物、一支紅光手電筒

materials.en: A clipboard, a pencil, and a watch
materials.zh: 寫字板、鉛筆和手錶

steps.en: Pick a night marked Good in the list. Go with an adult to a dark, safe place away from roads and lights.
steps.zh: 挑清單上標示「好」的夜晚，和大人一起到遠離道路和燈光的暗處。

steps.en: Lie back and let your eyes adjust for 20 minutes. Use only red light to read and write.
steps.zh: 躺下來，讓眼睛適應 20 分鐘；看紙寫字只用紅光。

steps.en: For one hour, write down the time of each meteor and whether its path points back to the radiant.
steps.zh: 觀察一個小時：記下每顆流星出現的時間，以及它的路徑是否指向輻射點。

steps.en: Add up your meteors for every 15 minutes, then compare with your classmates. Did more appear later in the night?
steps.zh: 每 15 分鐘加總一次，再和同學比較：越晚是不是越多？

activities.tip_en: Safety tip: always go with an adult, dress warmly, and never watch from a road or a rooftop.
activities.tip_zh: 安全提示：一定要有大人陪同，穿暖一點，不要在馬路上或屋頂上觀察。

lessons.title: Why Are Stars Different Colors?
lessons.title_zh: 星星為什麼有不同的顏色？
lessons.blurb_en: Red Betelgeuse and blue-white Rigel sit in the same constellation. Heat a star from 2,000 to 30,000 degrees and watch its color change, then sort 580 real stars by color into the famous H-R diagram.
lessons.blurb_zh: 紅色的參宿四和藍白的參宿七在同一個星座裡。把一顆星從 2,000 度加熱到 30,000 度，看它怎麼變色；再把 580 顆真實的星依顏色排排站，排出有名的赫羅圖。
lessons.big_idea_en: A star's color tells us how hot its surface is. Cooler stars glow orange-red, hotter stars glow white and blue-white, and our Sun sits in the middle.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 星星的顏色告訴我們它的表面有多熱。比較冷的星發出橙紅色的光，比較熱的星是白色、藍白色，我們的太陽在中間。

lab.title_en: Heat a Star, Then Sort the Stars
lab.title_zh: 加熱一顆星，再讓星星排排站
lab.how_en: Drag the temperature slider and watch the star change from orange-red to white to blue-white, with the Sun beside it for comparison. On the right, see its light color by color: hotter stars shine brightest at shorter, bluer wavelengths. Then switch to Sort the Stars: about 580 real stars measured by Hipparcos start out in the sky around the Sun. Press the sort button, and they fly into place by color and true brightness.
lab.how_zh: 拉動溫度滑桿，看這顆星從橙紅變白、再變藍白，旁邊有一顆太陽對照。右邊把它的光一個顏色一個顏色攤開：越熱的星，最強的光越偏向波長短的藍色。再切換到「星星排排站」：依巴谷衛星量過的約 580 顆真實恆星，先在太陽周圍的天空中；按下排排站，它們就依顏色和真正的亮度飛到定位。

legend.en: Slider colors: the real color of a glowing object at each temperature
legend.zh: 滑桿上的顏色：每個溫度下發光物體真正的顏色

legend.en: Small star: the Sun, 5,772 K, for comparison
legend.zh: 小顆的星：太陽，5,772 K，對照用

legend.en: Sorted view: left is hotter, right is cooler; up is brighter, down is fainter
legend.zh: 排排站：左熱右冷，上亮下暗

legend.en: K is kelvin: subtract 273 for degrees Celsius
legend.zh: K 是絕對溫度（克耳文），減 273 就是攝氏度數

lab.scale_en: Colors are calculated from the physics of glowing objects (Planck's law) and turned into screen colors. In the sorted view, each star's color comes from its measured color index, and its height from its true brightness, using the Hipparcos distance. Before sorting, distances are squeezed so that faraway stars fit on the screen.
lab.scale_zh: 顏色是用發光物體的物理（普朗克定律）算出來、再換成螢幕顏色。排排站時，每顆星的顏色來自量到的色指數，高度來自它真正的亮度（用依巴谷衛星的距離換算）。排之前的距離有壓縮，遠方的星才放得進畫面。

paras: Look at Orion on a winter evening. Betelgeuse, on his shoulder, glows orange-red, while Rigel, at his foot, shines blue-white. Look carefully at other bright stars, and you will find that stars are not all white. They come in a whole range of colors: orange-red, orange, yellowish white, white, and blue-white. What makes the difference?

The answer is temperature. Anything hot enough gives off light, and its color depends on how hot it is. A piece of iron in a blacksmith's fire first glows dull red, then orange, then yellow, and finally white. A star's surface works the same way. Orange-red stars like Betelgeuse are the coolest, at about 3,300 degrees Celsius. Our Sun is about 5,500 degrees, and blue-white stars like Rigel are 12,000 degrees or more. This is the opposite of a bathroom faucet, where red means hot and blue means cold!

A star does not give off just one color. It gives off a whole rainbow of light mixed together, plus light our eyes cannot see. A hotter star gives off more blue light, and a cooler star gives off more red. The Sun's light is strongest in the green part of the rainbow, but it mixes in so much of every other color that the Sun is really white. It only looks yellow or orange when it is low in the sky, because the air scatters away some of its blue light.

About a hundred years ago, astronomers began sorting stars by their light. At Harvard, Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stars into classes named O, B, A, F, G, K, and M, from hottest to coolest. Then Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell compared each star's color with how bright it really is. Most stars fell along one band, now called the main sequence. A few were giants, far brighter than their color suggests because they are enormous, and a few were tiny, faint white dwarfs.

Chinese astronomers paid attention to star colors, too. More than 2,000 years ago, the historian Sima Qian used stars as color samples: white like Sirius, red like Antares, and yellow like Betelgeuse. Yellow? Today Betelgeuse is clearly orange-red. In 2022, a team of astronomers suggested that the ancient records are right and that Betelgeuse has slowly changed color as it aged into a red supergiant. Antares, the red heart of the Scorpion, was known in China as the Great Fire.

You can see star colors for yourself, but they are soft, because our eyes see color poorly in the dark. The trick is to compare: look from Betelgeuse to Rigel, or from Arcturus to Vega. A pair of binoculars, slightly out of focus, makes the colors easier to see. Use the list below to find tonight's bright stars over Changhua, sorted from the coolest to the hottest.
paras_zh: 冬天的傍晚看看獵戶座。他肩膀上的參宿四發出橙紅色的光，腳邊的參宿七卻是藍白色。仔細看看其他亮星，你會發現星星不全是白的，而是有一整排顏色：橙紅、橙、黃白、白、藍白。是什麼造成這些差別？
答案是溫度。任何東西只要夠熱就會發光，而光的顏色由它有多熱決定。鐵匠爐火裡的一塊鐵，先發出暗紅色的光，接著變橙、變黃，最後變白。星星的表面也是這樣。像參宿四這樣的橙紅色星最冷，大約攝氏 3,300 度；我們的太陽大約 5,500 度；像參宿七這樣的藍白色星有 12,000 度以上。這和浴室的水龍頭正好相反——水龍頭是紅色代表熱、藍色代表冷！
一顆星發出的不只一種顏色，而是把整道彩虹的光混在一起，還有眼睛看不見的光。越熱的星發出越多藍光，越冷的星發出越多紅光。太陽的光在彩虹的綠色部分最強，但它混進了大量其他顏色，所以太陽其實是白的。只有太陽低垂時看起來才偏黃或橙，因為空氣把它的一部分藍光散射掉了。
大約一百年前，天文學家開始依星光替恆星分類。哈佛大學的坎農（Annie Jump Cannon）把幾十萬顆星分成 O、B、A、F、G、K、M 幾類，從最熱排到最冷。接著，赫茨普朗和羅素把每顆星的顏色和它真正的亮度放在一起比較，發現大部分的星都落在同一條帶子上，今天叫做「主序帶」。少數是巨星，比它的顏色該有的亮度亮得多，因為它們非常巨大；還有少數是又小又暗的白矮星。
中國的天文學家也很留意星星的顏色。兩千多年前，司馬遷在《史記．天官書》裡拿星星當顏色的樣本：「白比狼，赤比心，黃比參左肩」——白像天狼星、紅像心宿二、黃像參宿四。黃色？今天的參宿四明明是橙紅色。2022 年，一組天文學家認為古代紀錄沒有錯：參宿四在老化成紅超巨星的過程中，慢慢變了顏色。天蠍座紅色的心臟心宿二，在中國叫做「大火」。
你可以親眼看看星星的顏色，只是顏色很淡，因為眼睛在黑暗中分辨顏色的能力很差。訣竅是比較：從參宿四看到參宿七，或從大角星看到織女星。用雙筒望遠鏡、稍微失焦，顏色會比較明顯。用下面的清單找找今晚彰化天上的亮星，它們已經從最冷排到最熱。

palette.note_en: The most common kind of star: a small, cool red dwarf. Too faint to see without a telescope.
palette.note_zh: 最常見的一種星：又小又冷的紅矮星，肉眼看不到。

palette.note_en: A red supergiant so big that it would swallow Mars's orbit if it took the Sun's place.
palette.note_zh: 紅超巨星，大到如果放在太陽的位置，會吞掉火星的軌道。

palette.note_en: An orange giant, the brightest star in the spring sky. Compare it with blue-white Spica nearby.
palette.note_zh: 橙色巨星，春季夜空最亮的星。和附近藍白色的角宿一比一比。

palette.note_en: A middle-of-the-road star. Its light peaks in green, yet the mix looks white.
palette.note_zh: 一顆中等的星。它的光在綠色最強，混起來卻是白的。

palette.note_en: A little hotter than the Sun, and one of our near neighbors, 11.5 light-years away.
palette.note_zh: 比太陽稍熱，也是我們的近鄰，在 11.5 光年外。

palette.note_en: Sima Qian's sample of white. Low in the sky, it twinkles in flashes of many colors.
palette.note_zh: 司馬遷「白比狼」的白色樣本。低垂時會閃出各種顏色。

palette.note_en: Orion's blue-white foot, a supergiant more than 100,000 times as bright as the Sun.
palette.note_zh: 獵戶座藍白色的腳，是一顆比太陽亮十萬倍以上的超巨星。

palette.note_en: So hot that most of its light is ultraviolet, which our eyes cannot see.
palette.note_zh: 熱到大部分的光是紫外線，眼睛看不見。

lessons.palette_note_en: K means kelvin, the scientific temperature scale: subtract 273 to get degrees Celsius. The letter is the star's class, from hot O and B to cool K and M.
lessons.palette_note_zh: K 是絕對溫度（克耳文），減 273 就是攝氏度數。字母是光譜型，從熱的 O、B 排到冷的 K、M。

tonight.lead_zh: 今晚九點彰化天上的每一顆亮星，由冷排到熱，附上表面溫度。清單在瀏覽器裡照今天的日期現算。

culture_cards.lead_en: Long before thermometers, people noticed the colors of the stars and wrote them down.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 在溫度計發明之前很久，人們就注意到星星的顏色，還把它記了下來。

cards.quote_zh: 白比狼，赤比心，黃比參左肩，蒼比參右肩，黑比奎大星。——《史記．天官書》
cards.quote_en: "White like Sirius, red like Antares, yellow like Betelgeuse, blue like Bellatrix, black like the great star of Kui." (Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian)
cards.body_en: Sima Qian used bright stars to describe the colors of the planets. His yellow Betelgeuse helped astronomers in 2022 argue that the star has turned red in the last 2,000 years.
cards.body_zh: 司馬遷用亮星來描述行星的顏色。他筆下黃色的參宿四，成了 2022 年天文學家主張「這顆星兩千年來變紅了」的證據之一。

cards.en: The Red Heart of the Scorpion
cards.quote_zh: 七月流火，九月授衣。——《詩經．豳風．七月》
cards.quote_en: "In the seventh month, the Fire flows west; in the ninth month, we hand out winter clothes." (Book of Songs)
cards.body_en: The Fire is Antares, red as a flame. "The Fire flows" means it sinks lower in the west each evening as autumn comes, so the line is about cooling weather, not a heat wave.
cards.body_zh: 「火」是心宿二（大火），紅得像火焰。「流火」是說它在傍晚一天比一天低、往西沉落，表示秋天要來、天氣轉涼，不是形容天氣炎熱。

cards.body_en: The name Antares comes from Greek for "rival of Ares," the god the Romans called Mars, because its red color matches the red planet. Every two years or so, Mars passes near Antares, and the two red lights can be compared side by side.
cards.body_zh: Antares（心宿二）的名字來自希臘文「Ares（羅馬人稱 Mars，火星）的對手」，因為它和紅色的火星一樣紅。火星每隔約兩年經過它附近，兩點紅光可以並排比較——中國古人叫這種天象「熒惑守心」（第七課）。

cards.body_en: In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon and her team at Harvard sorted the light of hundreds of thousands of stars by hand. Her order, O B A F G K M, is still used today. Students remember it with "Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me" or "Oh Be A Fine Guy, Kiss Me."
cards.body_zh: 二十世紀初，哈佛大學的坎農和她的團隊用肉眼一張張判讀了幾十萬顆星的光譜。她排出的順序 O B A F G K M 沿用至今，英文口訣是「Oh Be A Fine Girl（或 Guy）, Kiss Me」。

myths.myth_en: Red means hot and blue means cold, like a faucet.
myths.myth_zh: 紅色代表熱、藍色代表冷，就像水龍頭。
myths.fact_en: For glowing objects, it is the other way around. Red stars are the coolest, and blue-white stars are the hottest.
myths.fact_zh: 發光的東西正好相反：紅色的星最冷，藍白色的星最熱。

myths.myth_en: The Sun is a yellow star.
myths.myth_zh: 太陽是黃色的星。
myths.fact_en: Seen from space, the Sun is white. It looks yellow or orange only through our air, especially when it is low in the sky.
myths.fact_zh: 從太空看，太陽是白色的。只有隔著大氣看，特別是太陽低垂的時候，才會偏黃或偏橙。

myths.myth_en: Some stars are green.
myths.myth_zh: 有些星星是綠色的。
myths.fact_en: A star whose light peaks in green, like the Sun, also gives off plenty of every other color, and the mix looks white. There are no green stars.
myths.fact_zh: 光在綠色最強的星（像太陽）也發出大量其他顏色，混在一起是白色。沒有綠色的星。

myths.myth_en: A star flashing red and blue near the horizon is changing color.
myths.myth_zh: 地平線附近一閃紅一閃藍的星，正在變色。
myths.fact_en: Our moving air bends each color of starlight a little differently. Near the horizon, a bright star like Sirius twinkles in flashes of color, but the star itself stays the same.
myths.fact_zh: 流動的空氣把星光的每種顏色折射得不太一樣。在地平線附近，天狼星這樣的亮星會一閃一閃地變色，但星星本身沒有變。

tricks.title_en: Red is cool, blue is hot
tricks.body_en: For stars, red means cooler and blue-white means hotter, the opposite of a faucet.
tricks.body_zh: 星星的紅色比較冷、藍白色比較熱，和水龍頭相反。

tricks.title_en: O B A F G K M
tricks.title_zh: O B A F G K M
tricks.body_en: From hottest to coolest: Oh Be A Fine Girl (or Guy), Kiss Me.
tricks.body_zh: 從最熱到最冷。英文口訣：Oh Be A Fine Girl（或 Guy）, Kiss Me。

tricks.title_en: The Sun is in the middle
tricks.body_en: About 5,500 degrees Celsius, a G star: not the hottest, not the coolest.
tricks.body_zh: 大約攝氏 5,500 度，G 型星：不是最熱，也不是最冷。

tricks.body_en: Red Betelgeuse on the shoulder, blue-white Rigel at the foot: compare them on a winter night.
tricks.body_zh: 肩上紅色的參宿四、腳邊藍白的參宿七，冬夜比一比。

materials.en: The list of tonight's star colors on this page
materials.zh: 本頁「今晚星星的顏色」清單

materials.en: Crayons or colored pencils and a dark sheet of paper
materials.zh: 蠟筆或色鉛筆，以及一張深色的紙

materials.en: Binoculars, if you have them
materials.zh: 雙筒望遠鏡（有的話）

steps.en: With an adult, go outside on a clear evening and let your eyes adjust for 10 minutes.
steps.zh: 和大人一起在晴朗的傍晚到戶外，讓眼睛適應黑暗 10 分鐘。

steps.en: Find two bright stars from the list, one cool and one hot. Look back and forth between them.
steps.zh: 從清單裡找兩顆亮星，一顆冷、一顆熱，來回比較著看。

steps.en: If you have binoculars, turn the focus a little so each star becomes a small disk. The colors will be easier to see.
steps.zh: 有雙筒望遠鏡的話，把焦距稍微轉開，讓星星變成小圓盤，顏色會更明顯。

steps.en: Draw each star with the color you saw, then check its temperature in the list. Did the coolest star look the reddest?
steps.zh: 用你看到的顏色把每顆星畫下來，再對照清單上的溫度：最冷的星看起來最紅嗎？

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: then drag the temperature slider in the 3D model to each star's temperature and compare the screen color with your drawing.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：接著把 3D 模型的溫度滑桿拉到每顆星的溫度，比較螢幕上的顏色和你畫的。

materials.en: A large poster with two arrows: hotter to cooler (left to right) and fainter to brighter (bottom to top)
materials.zh: 一張大海報，畫兩個箭頭：由左到右是由熱到冷，由下到上是由暗到亮

materials.en: Sticky dots in red, orange, yellow, white, and blue
materials.zh: 紅、橙、黃、白、藍各色圓點貼紙

materials.en: Star cards with each star's temperature and true brightness (the cards on this page, plus a few more)
materials.zh: 寫著溫度與真正亮度的星星卡（本頁的卡片，再加幾顆）

steps.en: Give each student or pair one or two star cards.
steps.zh: 每位同學或每組拿一、兩張星星卡。

steps.en: Choose the dot color that matches the star's temperature, and stick it on the poster in the right place.
steps.zh: 依星星的溫度挑顏色相符的貼紙，貼到海報上對的位置。

steps.en: When everyone is done, step back. Do most dots fall along a band from the upper left to the lower right?
steps.zh: 全部貼完後退後看：大部分的點是不是從左上排到右下，成一條帶子？

steps.en: Find the dots that are off the band. Which are giants, and which are white dwarfs?
steps.zh: 找出不在帶子上的點：哪些是巨星？哪些是白矮星？

activities.tip_en: Teaching tip: then press the sort button in the 3D model and watch 580 real stars build the same diagram.
activities.tip_zh: 教學提示：接著按 3D 模型的「排排站」，看 580 顆真實的星排出同一張圖。

lessons.title: Why Do We Always See the Same Side of the Moon?
lessons.title_zh: 月亮為什麼總是同一面對著我們？
lessons.blurb_en: The Moon does spin: exactly once for every trip around Earth. Switch its spin off or speed it up and see what Earth would see, then find out how the real Moon is tipped today.
lessons.blurb_zh: 月亮其實會自轉：繞地球一圈，正好自轉一圈。把它的自轉關掉或加快，看看地球會看到什麼；再看看今天真實的月亮微微轉向哪一邊。
lessons.big_idea_en: The Moon spins exactly once for every trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us. Long ago, Earth's tides slowed the Moon's spin until the two times matched.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 月亮繞地球一圈，正好自轉一圈，所以永遠同一面朝向我們。很久以前，地球的潮汐作用讓月亮越轉越慢，直到兩個時間一模一樣。

lab.title_en: One Spin for Every Trip Around Earth
lab.how_en: The red arrow sticks out of the middle of the Moon's near side. Press Play: in the real Moon, the arrow keeps pointing at Earth, and the small window on the right, the view from Earth, always shows the same face. Now switch the spin to No spin or Too fast and watch the far side come around. Turn on Exaggerate rocking to see how the real Moon sways a few degrees each month.
